Module 01 / Physics 2

Fluids: start with a force diagram

Density, pressure, hydraulics, and floating bodies.

Topics in this module
Density, relative density, and unit conversionsPressure and the hydrostatic derivationAtmospheric, gauge, absolute, and connected-column casesPascal's principle and hydraulic displacementArchimedes' principle: derive it before choosing a volumeFloating, sinking, and identifying unknown densitySource tables, pressure units, and the two air examplesMissing companion pressure and buoyancy problems

A fluid can flow. Liquids and gases are fluids. Fluid statics studies equilibrium; fluid dynamics studies motion. In the molecular model, gas particles are widely separated and compressible. A liquid has a definite volume but takes its container's shape. The hydrostatic formulas below require a stationary fluid, not an accelerating flow.

Density, relative density, and unit conversions

Density measures mass per volume. Relative density compares two densities and has no unit. Use the fluid density in buoyancy calculations, not the object's density.

ρ=mV,m=ρV,V=mρ,w=mg=ρVg,SG=ρρwater.\rho=\frac mV,\quad m=\rho V,\quad V=\frac m\rho,\quad w=mg=\rho Vg,\quad SG=\frac{\rho}{\rho_{water}}.ρ=Vm​,m=ρV,V=ρm​,w=mg=ρVg,SG=ρwater​ρ​.

For a composite body, divide the total mass by the total external volume. For separate parts with additive volumes, use ρavg=∑m∑V\rho _{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\sum m}{\sum V}ρavg​=∑V∑m​. A hollow object's average density includes its empty interior. Water is about 1000 kgm31000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1000m3kg​ in the classroom model. Convert 1gcm3\frac{1 g}{\mathrm{cm}^{3}}cm31g​ to 1000 kgm31000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1000m3kg​. Also use 1L=10−3 m31 L = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}1L=10−3m3, 1 mL=1 cm31\,\mathrm{mL} = 1\,\mathrm{cm}^{3}1mL=1cm3, and 1 cm3=10−6 m31\,\mathrm{cm}^{3} = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}1cm3=10−6m3. Squaring and cubing conversion factors is essential.

Worked example — primary p. 10. A room measures 4.0×5.0×3.0 m4.0 \times 5.0 \times 3.0\,\mathrm{m}4.0×5.0×3.0m. With ρair=1.20 kgm3\rho _{\mathrm{air}} = 1.20\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}ρair​=1.20m3kg​, V=60 m3V = 60\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=60m3. Therefore m=1.20×60=72 kgm = 1.20 \times 60 = 72\,\mathrm{kg}m=1.20×60=72kg. Its weight is 72×9.81=706.32 N72 \times 9.81 = 706.32\,\mathrm{N}72×9.81=706.32N. Mass and weight have different units.

Pressure and the hydrostatic derivation

Pressure is normal force per area: P=F⊥AP = \frac{F_{\perp}}{A}P=AF⊥​​. One pascal equals one Nm2\frac{N}{m^{2}}m2N​. Rearrange to F⊥=PAF_{\perp} = PAF⊥​=PA or A=F⊥PA = \frac{F_{\perp}}{P}A=PF⊥​​. Pressure is a scalar; the force on each wall points perpendicular to that wall. A static fluid cannot sustain a shear stress.

Derivation. Isolate a vertical fluid column of area A and depth h. The downward forces are P0AP_{0} AP0​A and its weight ρAhg\rho AhgρAhg. The upward force is PbottomA. Equilibrium gives:

PbA−P0A−ρAhg=0⇒Pb=P0+ρgh.P_bA-P_0A-\rho Ahg=0\Rightarrow P_b=P_0+\rho gh.Pb​A−P0​A−ρAhg=0⇒Pb​=P0​+ρgh.

The area cancels. This explains why pressure at a given depth does not depend on container shape. Equal pressure at equal depth requires the same connected, stationary fluid under the same surface conditions.

ΔP=ρgh,h=ΔPρg,ρ=ΔPgh,F=(P0+ρgh)A.\Delta P=\rho gh,\quad h=\frac{\Delta P}{\rho g},\quad \rho=\frac{\Delta P}{gh},\quad F=(P_0+\rho gh)A.ΔP=ρgh,h=ρgΔP​,ρ=ghΔP​,F=(P0​+ρgh)A.

Pressure differences across a wall use the pressure on BOTH sides. Do not multiply an absolute pressure by area when the question asks the net force against outside air. For nonconstant density, the general vertical relation is dPdz=−ρ(z)g\frac{dP}{dz} = - \rho \left( z \right) gdzdP​=−ρ(z)g; integrate instead of assuming ρgh\rho ghρgh.

Worked example — diver, primary p. 17. At 20 m20\,\mathrm{m}20m in freshwater, Pgauge=1000×9.8×20=196,000 PaP_{\mathrm{gauge}} = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 196{,}000\,\mathrm{Pa}Pgauge​=1000×9.8×20=196,000Pa. Add 101,300 Pa101{,}300\,\mathrm{Pa}101,300Pa for an absolute pressure of 297,300 Pa297{,}300\,\mathrm{Pa}297,300Pa. The statement “pressure due to water” means the gauge contribution here.

Worked example — two liquids, primary p. 19. At 3.00 m3.00\,\mathrm{m}3.00m and g=9.81 ms2g = 9.81\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}}g=9.81s2m​, freshwater gives 130,730 Pa130{,}730\,\mathrm{Pa}130,730Pa absolute. Seawater with ρ=1030\rho = 1030ρ=1030 gives 131,612.9 Pa131{,}612.9\,\mathrm{Pa}131,612.9Pa. Their difference is 882.9 Pa882.9\,\mathrm{Pa}882.9Pa, because the same atmospheric term cancels.

Atmospheric, gauge, absolute, and connected-column cases

Pabs=Patm+Pg,Pg=Pabs−Patm.P_{abs}=P_{atm}+P_g,\quad P_g=P_{abs}-P_{atm}.Pabs​=Patm​+Pg​,Pg​=Pabs​−Patm​.

The slides use 1 atm≈101.3 kPa=760 torr≈760 mmHg1\,\mathrm{atm} \approx 101.3\,\mathrm{kPa} = 760\,\mathrm{torr} \approx 760\,\mathrm{mmHg}1atm≈101.3kPa=760torr≈760mmHg. Gauge pressure can be negative; absolute pressure cannot be negative. Vacuum devices do not create a pulling pressure. A pressure difference lets the higher-pressure surroundings push inward.

For a manometer, start at a known pressure. Add ρgΔh\rho g\Delta hρgΔh when moving DOWN through a fluid. Subtract it when moving UP. Keep each fluid's density separate. Set pressures equal at the same level only within the same connected fluid. For multiple stationary layers, Pbottom=Ptop+∑ρighiP_{\mathrm{bottom}} = P_{\mathrm{top}} + \sum \rho_{i} gh_{i}Pbottom​=Ptop​+∑ρi​ghi​.

Worked example — companion p. 6 type. A closed water column's gas interface is 0.60 m0.60\,\mathrm{m}0.60m below an open water surface. Pgas=101,300+1000×9.81×0.60=107,186 PaP_{\mathrm{gas}} = 101{,}300 + 1000 \times 9.81 \times 0.60 = 107{,}186\,\mathrm{Pa}Pgas​=101,300+1000×9.81×0.60=107,186Pa, about 1.058 atm1.058\,\mathrm{atm}1.058atm. A different interface height reverses the sign. The drawing, not the word “closed,” decides the height contribution.

Pascal's principle and hydraulic displacement

An applied pressure change travels through a confined fluid. At equal piston elevations and neglecting friction, ΔP1=ΔP2\Delta P_{1} = \Delta P_{2}ΔP1​=ΔP2​:

F1A1=F2A2,F2=F1A2A1=F1(r2r1)2.\frac{F_1}{A_1}=\frac{F_2}{A_2},\quad F_2=F_1\frac{A_2}{A_1}=F_1\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^2.A1​F1​​=A2​F2​​,F2​=F1​A1​A2​​=F1​(r1​r2​​)2.

Derive the distance relation. Conservation of incompressible fluid volume gives A1d1=A2d2A_{1} d_{1} = A_{2} d_{2}A1​d1​=A2​d2​. Thus d2d1=A1A2\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}} = \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}d1​d2​​=A2​A1​​. Multiplying by the force ratio gives F1d1=F2d2F_{1} d_{1} = F_{2} d_{2}F1​d1​=F2​d2​: force multiplication is not energy creation. For unequal piston heights, include the hydrostatic pressure difference before applying the force balance.

Worked example — primary p. 23. A 10,000 N10{,}000\,\mathrm{N}10,000N load sits on a piston of radius 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m. The smaller radius is 0.050 m0.050\,\mathrm{m}0.050m. Required input force: 10,000(0.0501.00)2=25 N10{,}000 \left( \frac{0.050}{1.00} \right)^{2} = 25\,\mathrm{N}10,000(1.000.050​)2=25N. A diameter ratio gives the same squared ratio if both inputs are diameters.

Worked example — companion p. 7. Diameters 5 cm5\,\mathrm{cm}5cm and 25 cm25\,\mathrm{cm}25cm give an area ratio of 25. An input of 100 N100\,\mathrm{N}100N produces 2500 N2500\,\mathrm{N}2500N ideally. The large piston moves only 125\frac{1}{25}251​ of the smaller piston's distance.

Archimedes' principle: derive it before choosing a volume

Pressure at a submerged block's bottom exceeds the pressure at its top. For constant area A, the net upward fluid force is (Pbottom−Ptop)A=ρfg(hbottom−htop)A\left( P_{\mathrm{bottom}} - P_{\mathrm{top}} \right) A = \rho_{f} g \left( h_{\mathrm{bottom}} - h_{\mathrm{top}} \right) A(Pbottom​−Ptop​)A=ρf​g(hbottom​−htop​)A. Since AΔh=VdisplacedA\Delta h = V_{\mathrm{displaced}}AΔh=Vdisplaced​:

FB=ρfgVdisp.F_B=\rho_f gV_{disp}.FB​=ρf​gVdisp​.

This relation uses the volume of displaced fluid. For a fully submerged impermeable body, it equals the object's external volume. For partial immersion, it does not equal the whole object volume. A fluid's pressure gradient produces buoyancy even without a free surface immediately beside the object.

For a hanging object in equilibrium, T+FB−mg=0T + F_{B} - mg = 0T+FB​−mg=0, so T=mg−FBT = mg - F_{B}T=mg−FB​. Apparent weight equals that tension. If a light object is tied DOWN, FB−mg−T=0F_{B} - mg - T = 0FB​−mg−T=0, so T=FB−mgT = F_{B} - mgT=FB​−mg. Choose the sign from the diagram.

Worked example — primary p. 32 type. A 2.00 kg2.00\,\mathrm{kg}2.00kg brass block has density 8700 kgm38700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}8700m3kg​ and is fully submerged in water. V=28700=2.299×10−4 m3V = \frac{2}{8700} = 2.299 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=87002​=2.299×10−4m3. FB=2.255 NF_{B} = 2.255\,\mathrm{N}FB​=2.255N. Its upward-string tension is 19.62−2.255=17.365 N19.62 - 2.255 = 17.365\,\mathrm{N}19.62−2.255=17.365N. The density is the chosen brass-table value; a different supplied value changes the result.

Worked example — companion pp. 9–10. A 0.10 m0.10\,\mathrm{m}0.10m cube of wood has density 700 kgm3700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}700m3kg​. V=0.001 m3V = 0.001\,\mathrm{m}^{3}V=0.001m3, mg=6.867 Nmg = 6.867\,\mathrm{N}mg=6.867N, and FB=9.81 NF_{B} = 9.81\,\mathrm{N}FB​=9.81N. A bottom string must pull downward with 2.943 N2.943\,\mathrm{N}2.943N. A negative “upward tension” would indicate the wrong assumed string direction.

Floating, sinking, and identifying unknown density

For free floating equilibrium, FB=mgF_{B} = mgFB​=mg. With m=ρobjectVtotalm = \rho _{\mathrm{object}}V_{\mathrm{total}}m=ρobject​Vtotal​:

VsubVtotal=ρobjectρf,ρf=ρobjectVtotalVsub.\frac{V_{sub}}{V_{total}}=\frac{\rho_{object}}{\rho_f},\quad \rho_f=\rho_{object}\frac{V_{total}}{V_{sub}}.Vtotal​Vsub​​=ρf​ρobject​​,ρf​=ρobject​Vsub​Vtotal​​.

This fraction must lie between zero and one. If the average object density exceeds the fluid density, a freely floating equilibrium with partial immersion is impossible. A sinking object still has an upward buoyant force; that force is simply insufficient to balance its weight. Neutral buoyancy means equal average densities, not zero buoyancy.

Worked example — primary p. 34. One-third of a person's volume is above the surface, so two-thirds is submerged. With average density 970 kgm3970\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}970m3kg​, fluid density: 970(23)=1455 kgm3\frac{970}{\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)} = 1455\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}(32​)970​=1455m3kg​. The printed 1460 is a rounded value. The assumed 3 m33\,\mathrm{m}^{3}3m3 is only a convenient volume ratio, not a realistic measured body volume.

Take note. Primary p. 12 labels density with Pa; its unit must be kgm3\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{m^{3}}m3kg​. Floating formulas require equilibrium without an extra vertical support force. Do not use them for a block held underwater by a string.

Derivation extension — weighing an unknown solid. Measure the weight Wair in air, then the apparent weight Wsub while fully submerged. Neglect air buoyancy and string mass. The difference is the fluid buoyancy: Wair−Wsub=ρfgVW_{\mathrm{air}} - W_{\mathrm{sub}} = \rho_{f} gVWair​−Wsub​=ρf​gV. Meanwhile Wair=ρobjectgVW_{\mathrm{air}} = \rho _{\mathrm{object}} gVWair​=ρobject​gV. Divide the equations to remove both g and V:

ρobject=ρfWairWair−Wsub.\rho_{object}=\rho_f\frac{W_{air}}{W_{air}-W_{sub}}.ρobject​=ρf​Wair​−Wsub​Wair​​.

For Wair=12.0 NW_{\mathrm{air}} = 12.0\,\mathrm{N}Wair​=12.0N and Wsub=8.0 NW_{\mathrm{sub}} = 8.0\,\mathrm{N}Wsub​=8.0N in water, density: 1000(12)(12−8)=3000 kgm3\frac{1000 \left( 12 \right)}{\left( 12 - 8 \right)} = 3000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}(12−8)1000(12)​=3000m3kg​. A smaller apparent weight means a larger buoyant force. This formula does not apply unchanged to an object resting on the bottom.

Worked extension — a layered column. An open tank holds 0.20 m0.20\,\mathrm{m}0.20m of oil, density 800 kgm3800\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}800m3kg​, above 0.30 m0.30\,\mathrm{m}0.30m of water. Gauge pressure at the bottom is 800(9.81)(0.20)+1000(9.81)(0.30)=4512.6 Pa800 \left( 9.81 \right) \left( 0.20 \right) + 1000 \left( 9.81 \right) \left( 0.30 \right) = 4512.6\,\mathrm{Pa}800(9.81)(0.20)+1000(9.81)(0.30)=4512.6Pa. A small horizontal bottom hatch of area 0.010 m20.010\,\mathrm{m}^{2}0.010m2, exposed to air underneath, feels a net downward force of 45.126 N45.126\,\mathrm{N}45.126N. Atmospheric pressure cancels across the hatch. For a tall vertical hatch, pressure varies over its area; use F=∫PdepthdAF = \int P_{\mathrm{depth}} dAF=∫Pdepth​dA, not the pressure at its lowest point everywhere.

These are the source's classroom values. Temperature and composition affect real densities. The brass example below uses the explicit 8700 kgm38700\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}8700m3kg​ value from p. 9.

Why a fluid has pressure — companion pp. 3–4. Molecular motion and interactions transfer momentum to container walls. Gravity creates a vertical pressure gradient, but it is not the only cause of pressure. Gas molecules still collide with walls in weightlessness. Over a small laboratory height, a gas's gravitational pressure change can be small; atmospheric pressure changes substantially over larger heights. Internal and external pressure partly balance around the body, so atmospheric pressure does not act as an unopposed inward force everywhere.

Relative-density check. Steel: SG=78001000=7.80SG = \frac{7800}{1000} = 7.80SG=10007800​=7.80. Brass: SG=87001000=8.70SG = \frac{8700}{1000} = 8.70SG=10008700​=8.70. Wood: SG=5001000=0.500SG = \frac{500}{1000} = 0.500SG=1000500​=0.500. Relative density has no kgm3\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{m^{3}}m3kg​ unit because the density units cancel.

Air in a room: distinguish the primary and companion problems

Sources: Primary p. 10; companion p. 2. Find: The air mass, then its weight.

  1. Use the primary dimensions 4.0×5.0×3.0 m4.0 \times 5.0 \times 3.0\,\mathrm{m}4.0×5.0×3.0m. Their product is 60 m360\,\mathrm{m}^{3}60m3.
  2. Use its 20°C air density: m=ρV=1.20(60)=72 kgm = \rho V = 1.20 \left( 60 \right) = 72\,\mathrm{kg}m=ρV=1.20(60)=72kg.
  3. Calculate weight separately: W=mg=72(9.81)=706.32 NW = mg = 72 \left( 9.81 \right) = 706.32\,\mathrm{N}W=mg=72(9.81)=706.32N.
  4. Use the companion dimensions 4.0×6.0×2.5 m4.0 \times 6.0 \times 2.5\,\mathrm{m}4.0×6.0×2.5m. Their product also equals 60 m360\,\mathrm{m}^{3}60m3.
  5. Use the companion's 0°C table: m=1.29(60)=77.4 kgm = 1.29 \left( 60 \right) = 77.4\,\mathrm{kg}m=1.29(60)=77.4kg, which rounds to 77 kg77\,\mathrm{kg}77kg.

Check. The volumes agree, but the selected air densities differ. The two mass answers therefore do not contradict each other.

Pressure at the closed end of the water tube

Source: Companion p. 6. Given: Open surface height 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m; closed-end height 0.40 m0.40\,\mathrm{m}0.40m above the same reference. Surface pressure is 1 atm1\,\mathrm{atm}1atm.

A fully submerged block: buoyancy, apparent weight, and sinking

Source: Companion p. 9. Given: Displaced volume 0.020 m30.020\,\mathrm{m}^{3}0.020m3; water density 1000 kgm31000\,\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{3}}1000m3kg​; block weight 250 N250\,\mathrm{N}250N. Use g=9.8 ms2g = 9.8\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}}g=9.8s2m​.

Module 02 / Physics 2

Thermal physics: separate heat, temperature, and internal energy

Expansion, heat, phase changes, and energy balances.

Topics in this module
Temperature scales and differencesLinear, area, and volume expansion: derivations and inversesContainers, overflow, water's anomaly, and phase diagramsHeat transfer, specific heat, and thermal equilibriumMixing: derive the common final temperatureLatent heat and every stage of an ice-to-steam problemFirst law and two sign conventionsMaterial tables, thermometer operation, and phase diagramsComplete the heat and mixing problems from both decksFirst-law cases, heating curves, and conduction calculations

Temperature describes thermal state. Heat Q is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Internal energy U belongs to the system. Heat is not a stored substance or another name for U. Work is a different mode of energy transfer. The source sometimes uses these terms interchangeably; the notes keep them separate.

Temperature scales and differences

TK=TC+273.15,TF=95TC+32,TC=59(TF−32).T_K=T_C+273.15,\quad T_F=\frac95T_C+32,\quad T_C=\frac59(T_F-32).TK​=TC​+273.15,TF​=59​TC​+32,TC​=95​(TF​−32).

Derivation. Water's standard freezing/boiling interval spans 100 Celsius degrees and 180 Fahrenheit degrees. The slope is 180100=95\frac{180}{100} = \frac{9}{5}100180​=59​. The freezing-point offset supplies 32. Kelvin uses the same interval size as Celsius but a different zero.

ΔTK=ΔTC,ΔTF=95ΔTC.\Delta T_K=\Delta T_C,\quad \Delta T_F=\frac95\Delta T_C.ΔTK​=ΔTC​,ΔTF​=59​ΔTC​.

Do not add 273.15 to a temperature CHANGE. A 20°C rise is a 20 K20\,\mathrm{K}20K rise, not 293.15 K293.15\,\mathrm{K}293.15K. Gas-law absolute-temperature ratios require Kelvin. Absolute zero does not mean every quantum-mechanical contribution to energy vanishes.

Thermometers measure temperature through a calibrated property, such as a liquid's volume, gas pressure, or electrical resistance. Mercury's illustrated −39°C to 357°C liquid range explains one thermometer limitation; it is not a universal temperature scale limit.

Linear, area, and volume expansion: derivations and inverses

For moderate changes with approximately constant coefficient, ΔL=αL0ΔT\Delta L = \alpha L_{0} \Delta TΔL=αL0​ΔT and L=L0(1+αΔT)L = L_{0} \left( 1 + \alpha \Delta T \right)L=L0​(1+αΔT). The coefficient has units K−1K^{-1}K−1 or °C−1C^{-1}C−1.

α=L−L0L0ΔT,ΔT=L−L0αL0,L0=L1+αΔT.\alpha=\frac{L-L_0}{L_0\Delta T},\quad \Delta T=\frac{L-L_0}{\alpha L_0},\quad L_0=\frac{L}{1+\alpha\Delta T}.α=L0​ΔTL−L0​​,ΔT=αL0​L−L0​​,L0​=1+αΔTL​.

Derive area expansion. Expand both dimensions by the same factor: AA0=(1+αΔT)2=1+2αΔT+α2ΔT2\begin{aligned}\frac{A}{A_{0}} &= \left( 1 + \alpha \Delta T \right)^{2} \\&= 1 + 2 \alpha \Delta T + \alpha^{2} \Delta T^{2}\end{aligned}A0​A​​=(1+αΔT)2=1+2αΔT+α2ΔT2​ Neglect the second-order term only when ∣αΔT∣≪1\left| \alpha \Delta T \right| \ll 1∣αΔT∣≪1. Then ΔA≈2αA0ΔT\Delta A \approx 2 \alpha A_{0} \Delta TΔA≈2αA0​ΔT. The slides call the area coefficient γ\gammaγ; γ≈2α\gamma \approx 2 \alphaγ≈2α.

Derive volume expansion. Three dimensions give VV0=(1+αΔT)3\frac{V}{V_{0}} = \left( 1 + \alpha \Delta T \right)^{3}V0​V​=(1+αΔT)3. Its first-order term is 1+3αΔT1 + 3 \alpha \Delta T1+3αΔT. Thus β≈3α\beta \approx 3 \alphaβ≈3α for an isotropic solid, and ΔV≈βV0ΔT\Delta V \approx \beta V_{0} \Delta TΔV≈βV0​ΔT. Liquids have their own volume coefficient; do not assign them a solid'sαs \alphasα without justification. The finite-power expressions follow the linear dimensional model; a temperature-dependent instantaneous coefficient requires integration.

A hole expands as the surrounding material would expand if the hole were filled with the same material. Heating both a plug and hole made from the same material does not automatically create clearance. Cooling only the plug or heating only the plate changes their relative fit.

Worked example — primary p. 11. A 50 m50\,\mathrm{m}50m steel tape at 20°C has α=11×10−6 K−1\alpha = 11 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}α=11×10−6K−1. At 35°C, ΔL=0.00825 m\Delta L = 0.00825\,\mathrm{m}ΔL=0.00825m and L=50.00825 mL = 50.00825\,\mathrm{m}L=50.00825m. The printed 50.008 m50.008\,\mathrm{m}50.008m is rounded. A hot tape has wider-spaced markings; distinguish the indicated reading from the actual length.

Containers, overflow, water's anomaly, and phase diagrams

For a full container and a small common temperature rise:

ΔVoverflow=V0(βliquid−βcontainer)ΔT.\Delta V_{overflow}=V_0(\beta_{liquid}-\beta_{container})\Delta T.ΔVoverflow​=V0​(βliquid​−βcontainer​)ΔT.

Derivation. Subtract the expanded container capacity V0(1+βcontainerΔT)V_{0} \left( 1 + \beta _{\mathrm{container}}\Delta T \right)V0​(1+βcontainer​ΔT) from the expanded liquid volume V0(1+βliquidΔT)V_{0} \left( 1 + \beta _{\mathrm{liquid}}\Delta T \right)V0​(1+βliquid​ΔT). The original V0V_{0}V0​ terms cancel. A negative result means no positive overflow in this model; the liquid leaves space instead.

Worked example — primary p. 18. V0=200 cm3V_{0} = 200\,\mathrm{cm}^{3}V0​=200cm3; ΔT=80 K\Delta T = 80\,\mathrm{K}ΔT=80K; βHg=18×10−5 K−1\beta Hg = 18 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}βHg=18×10−5K−1; αglass=0.40×10−5 K−1\alpha _{\mathrm{glass}} = 0.40 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}αglass​=0.40×10−5K−1. Therefore βglass=1.20×10−5\beta _{\mathrm{glass}} = 1.20 \times 10^{-5}βglass​=1.20×10−5. Overflow: 200(18−1.2)×10−5×80=2.688 cm3200 \left( 18 - 1.2 \right) \times 10^{-5} \times 80 = 2.688\,\mathrm{cm}^{3}200(18−1.2)×10−5×80=2.688cm3. Keep volume units consistent; conversion to m3m^{3}m3 is not necessary when every volume uses cm3\mathrm{cm}^{3}cm3.

Companion extension. Water contracts when heated from about 0°C to 4°C at ordinary pressure. Its density reaches a maximum near 4°C. “All matter expands when heated” is not a universal law. A phase diagram plots pressure against temperature. Boundaries separate phases; the triple point joins three phases. A liquid–gas boundary ends at the critical point. Do not confuse a phase diagram with a heating curve.

Heat transfer, specific heat, and thermal equilibrium

Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions; metals also have mobile-electron contributions. Convection carries energy with bulk fluid motion. Radiation transfers electromagnetic energy and needs no material medium. The source's explanation that solid molecules are generally far apart is incorrect.

The zeroth law states: if A and B separately share thermal equilibrium with C, A and B share thermal equilibrium. Equality of temperature, not equal mass or equal internal energy, characterizes that equilibrium.

Q=mc(Tf−Ti),c=QmΔT,m=QcΔT,Tf=Ti+Qmc.Q=mc(T_f-T_i),\quad c=\frac{Q}{m\Delta T},\quad m=\frac{Q}{c\Delta T},\quad T_f=T_i+\frac{Q}{mc}.Q=mc(Tf​−Ti​),c=mΔTQ​,m=cΔTQ​,Tf​=Ti​+mcQ​.

The relation assumes no phase change and approximately constant c. Heat capacity C=mcC = mcC=mc has units JK\frac{J}{K}KJ​. Specific heat c has units J(kg⋅K)\frac{J}{\left( \mathrm{kg} \cdot K \right)}(kg⋅K)J​. With variable c, Q=m∫c(T)dTQ = m \int c \left( T \right) dTQ=m∫c(T)dT. The PDFs use 1 cal=4.186 J1\,\mathrm{cal} = 4.186\,\mathrm{J}1cal=4.186J and cwater=4186 JkgKc_{\mathrm{water}} = 4186\,\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K}}cwater​=4186kgKJ​. Use the supplied convention consistently. One kcal is 1000 cal1000\,\mathrm{cal}1000cal; the source uses 1 Btu≈252 cal1\,\mathrm{Btu} \approx 252\,\mathrm{cal}1Btu≈252cal.

Worked example — primary p. 32. Water of mass 0.625 kg0.625\,\mathrm{kg}0.625kg initially at 75°C loses 7.96×104 J7.96 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{J}7.96×104J. Use Q=−79,600 JQ = - 79{,}600\,\mathrm{J}Q=−79,600J. Tf=75−79,600(0.625×4186)≈44.575∘CT_{f} = 75 - \frac{79{,}600}{\left( 0.625 \times 4186 \right)} \approx 44.575^{\circ} CTf​=75−(0.625×4186)79,600​≈44.575∘C, about 44.6°C. A positive loss magnitude must acquire a negative sign in the system energy equation.

Mixing: derive the common final temperature

For an insulated mixture without phase changes, ∑mc(Tf−Ti)=0\sum mc \left( T_{f} - T_{i} \right) = 0∑mc(Tf​−Ti​)=0. Expand the sum and collect Tf:

Tf=∑imiciTi∑imici.T_f=\frac{\sum_i m_ic_iT_i}{\sum_i m_ic_i}.Tf​=∑i​mi​ci​∑i​mi​ci​Ti​​.

Include a calorimeter as another heat-capacity term if its energy is not negligible. Without phase change or external heating, Tf lies between the initial temperatures. That is a useful sign check.

Worked example — primary p. 33. Iron: 0.065 kg0.065\,\mathrm{kg}0.065kg at 525°C, c=444 JkgKc = 444\,\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K}}c=444kgKJ​. Water: 0.635 kg0.635\,\mathrm{kg}0.635kg at 15°C, c=4186c = 4186c=4186. The weighted formula gives Tf≈20.478∘CT_{f} \approx 20.478^{\circ} CTf​≈20.478∘C, about 20.5°C. Neither the simple arithmetic average nor the mass-weighted average alone is correct when c differs.

Latent heat and every stage of an ice-to-steam problem

During an equilibrium phase transition at the specified pressure, Q=±mLQ = \pm \mathrm{mL}Q=±mL. Melting and vaporization absorb heat; freezing and condensation release heat. Lf belongs to solid–liquid transitions. Lv belongs to liquid–gas transitions. Primary p. 38 incorrectly repeats melting/freezing labels for vaporization.

Decision method. Bring material to the phase boundary with mcΔTmc\Delta TmcΔT. Use mL for the transition. Then use the new phase's specific heat. Never apply a single water c across ice, liquid, and steam.

Worked example — primary p. 41. Convert 0.100 kg0.100\,\mathrm{kg}0.100kg of ice at −40°C to steam at 110°C. Use cice=2090c_{\mathrm{ice}} = 2090cice​=2090, cwater=4186c_{\mathrm{water}} = 4186cwater​=4186, csteam=2110 JkgKc_{\mathrm{steam}} = 2110\,\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K}}csteam​=2110kgKJ​, Lf=3.35×105L_{f} = 3.35 \times 10^{5}Lf​=3.35×105 and Lv=2.26×106 JkgL_{v} = 2.26 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg}}Lv​=2.26×106kgJ​.

Q=0.1(2090)(40)+0.1(335000)+0.1(4186)(100)+0.1(2260000)+0.1(2110)(10)=311830 J.Q=0.1(2090)(40)+0.1(335000)+0.1(4186)(100)+0.1(2260000)+0.1(2110)(10)=311830\ \mathrm J.Q=0.1(2090)(40)+0.1(335000)+0.1(4186)(100)+0.1(2260000)+0.1(2110)(10)=311830 J.

The five contributions are 8360, 33,500, 41,860, 226,000, and 2110 J2110\,\mathrm{J}2110J. The result rounds to 3.12×105 J3.12 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}3.12×105J. The latent-heat stage dominates here.

For ice mixed with warm water, compare the available cooling energy with mLfmL_fmLf​ before assuming all ice melts. If the energy is insufficient, the final mixture can stay at 0°C with some ice remaining. If all ice melts, subtract the melting energy before solving the later temperature rise. The companion's milk-and-ice case uses this energy-budget logic.

Worked extension — test the final phase first. Mix 0.050 kg0.050\,\mathrm{kg}0.050kg of ice at 0°C with 0.200 kg0.200\,\mathrm{kg}0.200kg of water at 30°C. Use cwater=4186c_{\mathrm{water}} = 4186cwater​=4186 and Lf=335,000L_{f} = 335{,}000Lf​=335,000 in SI units. The water can release 0.200(4186)(30)=25,116 J0.200 \left( 4186 \right) \left( 30 \right) = 25{,}116\,\mathrm{J}0.200(4186)(30)=25,116J before reaching 0°C. Melting all the ice needs 0.050(335,000)=16,750 J0.050 \left( 335{,}000 \right) = 16{,}750\,\mathrm{J}0.050(335,000)=16,750J. All the ice therefore melts. The remaining 8366 J8366\,\mathrm{J}8366J warms 0.250 kg0.250\,\mathrm{kg}0.250kg of liquid water, giving Tf=8366(0.250×4186)≈7.994∘CT_{f} = \frac{8366}{\left( 0.250 \times 4186 \right)} \approx 7.994^{\circ} CTf​=(0.250×4186)8366​≈7.994∘C.

Change only the ice mass to 0.100 kg0.100\,\mathrm{kg}0.100kg. Melting it all needs 33,500 J33{,}500\,\mathrm{J}33,500J, more than 25,116 J25{,}116\,\mathrm{J}25,116J. The final temperature stays 0°C. Melted mass: 25,116335,000≈0.07497 kg\frac{25{,}116}{335{,}000} \approx 0.07497\,\mathrm{kg}335,00025,116​≈0.07497kg; about 0.02503 kg0.02503\,\mathrm{kg}0.02503kg of ice remains. Do not report a negative final liquid temperature from an equation that incorrectly assumes complete melting.

First law and two sign conventions

The primary uses ΔU=Q−Wby\Delta U = Q - W_{\mathrm{by}}ΔU=Q−Wby​. The companion uses ΔU=Q+Won\Delta U = Q + W_{\mathrm{on}}ΔU=Q+Won​. They agree because Won=−WbyW_{\mathrm{on}} = - W_{\mathrm{by}}Won​=−Wby​. Q is positive into the system. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter; an isolated system exchanges neither.

Worked example — primary p. 45. Qnet=40−25=15 JQ_{\mathrm{net}} = 40 - 25 = 15\,\mathrm{J}Qnet​=40−25=15J. Wby,net=10−4=6 JW_{\mathrm{by,net}}=10-4=6\,\mathrm{J}Wby,net​=10−4=6J. ΔU=15−6=9 J\Delta U = 15 - 6 = 9\,\mathrm{J}ΔU=15−6=9J. Adding the 4 J4\,\mathrm{J}4J of compression to WbyW_{\mathrm{by}}Wby​ would reverse its meaning.

Companion example. Heat input 1500 J1500\,\mathrm{J}1500J, heat loss 400 J400\,\mathrm{J}400J, expansion work 600 J600\,\mathrm{J}600J, and paddle-wheel work ON the gas 250 J250\,\mathrm{J}250J give ΔU=1500−400−600+250=750 J\Delta U = 1500 - 400 - 600 + 250 = 750\,\mathrm{J}ΔU=1500−400−600+250=750J.

Extension — steady conduction. Fourier's one-dimensional law gives heat rate H=kA(Th−Tc)LH = \frac{kA \left( T_{h} - T_{c} \right)}{L}H=LkA(Th​−Tc​)​ for a uniform slab. Derive Q=HtQ = HtQ=Ht; rearrange k=HL(AΔT)k = \frac{HL}{\left( A\Delta T \right)}k=(AΔT)HL​. For stacked slabs, thermal resistance is L(kA)\frac{L}{\left( kA \right)}(kA)L​, so H=ΔT∑RthermalH = \frac{\Delta T}{\sum R_{\mathrm{thermal}}}H=∑Rthermal​ΔT​. This is the conduction relation shown in the scanned companion, not an electrical resistance formula.

Source problems · full working

Material tables, thermometer operation, and phase diagrams

The primary and companion decks use different rounded material coefficients. For example, the primary gives steel α=1.2×10−5 K−1\alpha = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}α=1.2×10−5K−1. The companion uses 1.1×10−5 K−11.1 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}1.1×10−5K−1. Use the coefficient stated in each problem.

Bimetallic strip. Two bonded metals have different expansion coefficients. Heating makes the higher-expansion metal occupy the outside of the bend. The strip therefore bends toward the lower-expansion metal. A thermostat uses the bend to operate a contact. A liquid thermometer instead uses a calibrated change in liquid volume.

Historical correction. The companion prints 1792 for Celsius's scale. Uppsala University dates his original scale to 1742. His original orientation differed from the modern Celsius convention.

Microscopic model. Solid particles vibrate around equilibrium positions. Liquid particles remain close but can rearrange. Gas particles are widely separated. “Temperature measures average kinetic energy” is a useful introductory model, especially for an ideal gas. It is not a universal formula for the total internal energy of every material.

Derivation∴

Derive the temperature-scale conversions from a straight line

Use TF=aTC+bT_{F} = aT_{C} + bTF​=aTC​+b for the two fixed points at standard pressure.

  1. Insert the freezing point: 32=a(0)+b32 = a \left( 0 \right) + b32=a(0)+b, so b=32b = 32b=32.
  2. Insert the boiling point: 212=100a+32212 = 100 a + 32212=100a+32.
  3. Subtract 32 and divide by 100: a=180100=95a = \frac{180}{100} = \frac{9}{5}a=100180​=59​.
  4. Subtract the relation at two temperatures. The constant offset cancels.
TF=95TC+32,TC=59(TF−32),ΔTF=95ΔTC.T_F=\frac95T_C+32, \qquad T_C=\frac59(T_F-32), \qquad \Delta T_F=\frac95\Delta T_C.TF​=59​TC​+32,TC​=95​(TF​−32),ΔTF​=59​ΔTC​.

For 37°C, TF=98.6∘FT_{F} = 98.6^{\circ} FTF​=98.6∘F and TK=310.15 KT_{K} = 310.15\,\mathrm{K}TK​=310.15K. For a 2°C increase, ΔTF=3.6∘F\Delta T_{F} = 3.6^{\circ} FΔTF​=3.6∘F and ΔTK=2 K\Delta T_{K} = 2\,\mathrm{K}ΔTK​=2K. Do not add 32 or 273.15 to a temperature difference.

Water phase diagram. The companion marks the triple point near 0.01°C and 0.006 atm0.006\,\mathrm{atm}0.006atm. Its critical point lies near 374°C and 218 atm218\,\mathrm{atm}218atm. The solid–liquid boundary has a negative slope in this region. Increasing pressure can favor the denser liquid over ordinary ice.

Carbon-dioxide phase diagram. The companion marks a triple point near −56°C and 5 atm5\,\mathrm{atm}5atm, and a critical point near 31°C and 73 atm73\,\mathrm{atm}73atm. At 1 atm1\,\mathrm{atm}1atm, solid CO₂ sublimes instead of passing through a stable liquid phase. The values on the diagram are rounded. A heating curve has different axes: temperature versus added energy or heating time.

Phase names. Melting: solid → liquid. Freezing: liquid → solid. Vaporization: liquid → gas. Condensation: gas → liquid. Sublimation: solid → gas. Deposition: gas → solid.

Worked solution↳

Derivation∴

Derive the changing density of an expanding body

Assume the mass stays constant and use V=V0(1+βΔT)V = V_{0} \left( 1 + \beta \Delta T \right)V=V0​(1+βΔT).

ρ=mV=mV0(1+βΔT)=ρ01+βΔT.\rho=\frac{m}{V}=\frac{m}{V_0(1+\beta\Delta T)} =\frac{\rho_0}{1+\beta\Delta T}.ρ=Vm​=V0​(1+βΔT)m​=1+βΔTρ0​​.

For small ∣βΔT∣\left| \beta \Delta T \right|∣βΔT∣, expand the reciprocal to first order: ρ≈ρ0(1−βΔT)\rho \approx \rho_{0} \left( 1 - \beta \Delta T \right)ρ≈ρ0​(1−βΔT). A positive volume expansion lowers density when mass stays fixed. This is an algebraic consequence of the source laws, not an additional universal constant−β- \beta−β assumption for water near 4°C.

First-law cases, heating curves, and conduction calculations

Worked solution↳

Separate heat from work in the source's conceptual cases

Source: Primary p. 43.

  • Soup on an electric stove receives energy through heat transfer from the hot pan.
  • Hands near a fire receive thermal radiation; warm-air convection can also contribute.
  • A re-entering spacecraft transfers macroscopic mechanical energy into internal energy through interaction with the atmosphere. Compression and drag are central; a hot atmosphere can also exchange heat with the surface.

Take note. A temperature increase alone does not tell you whether the energy enters as heat or as work. Specify the system and the transfer mechanism.

Worked solution↳

Complete the two first-law numerical cases

Primary p. 44: Q=+3000 JQ = + 3000\,\mathrm{J}Q=+3000J and Wby=+2500 JW_{\mathrm{by}} = + 2500\,\mathrm{J}Wby​=+2500J. Therefore ΔU=Q−Wby=+500 J\Delta U = Q - W_{\mathrm{by}} = + 500\,\mathrm{J}ΔU=Q−Wby​=+500J.

Primary p. 45: The net heat is 40−25=+15 J40 - 25 = + 15\,\mathrm{J}40−25=+15J. The net work by the system is 10−4=+6 J10 - 4 = + 6\,\mathrm{J}10−4=+6J. Therefore ΔU=15−6=+9 J\Delta U = 15 - 6 = + 9\,\mathrm{J}ΔU=15−6=+9J.

Companion p. 8; alternate companion p. 6: The net heat is 1500−400=1100 J1500 - 400 = 1100\,\mathrm{J}1500−400=1100J. The net work on the gas is −600+250=−350 J- 600 + 250 = - 350\,\mathrm{J}−600+250=−350J. Therefore ΔU=Q+Won=1100−350=+750 J\Delta U = Q + W_{\mathrm{on}} = 1100 - 350 = + 750\,\mathrm{J}ΔU=Q+Won​=1100−350=+750J.

Check. The primary and companion sign conventions agree. Their work variables have opposite definitions.

Derivation∴

Read the slope of a heating curve

During a single phase, Q=mcΔTQ = mc\Delta TQ=mcΔT. At fixed m and approximately constant c, ΔTΔQ=1(mc)\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta Q} = \frac{1}{\left( mc \right)}ΔQΔT​=(mc)1​. A larger heat capacity produces a flatter temperature-versus-energy slope. During an equilibrium phase change, the added energy changes phase fraction, so the temperature plateau has slope zero.

For heating at constant power P, Q=PtQ = PtQ=Pt. Thus dTdt=P(mc)\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{P}{\left( mc \right)}dtdT​=(mc)P​ within a phase, and a complete phase transition takes Δt=mLP\Delta t = \frac{\mathrm{mL}}{P}Δt=PmL​. These relations require negligible energy losses and the stated constant-power model.

Module 03 / Physics 2

Electric charge and force: signs before substitution

Charging, Coulomb forces, vectors, and source-label corrections.

Topics in this module
Quantization, conservation, and charging mechanismsCoulomb's law: empirical starting law and algebraic formsSuperposition in one, two, and three dimensionsRectangles, diagonals, and force cancellationCharging diagrams and charge-conservation calculationsComplete the source force problems in one and two dimensions

Charge is a property of matter, not a synonym for “electron.” Electrons carry −e, protons +e, and neutrons zero net charge. Use e=1.602×10−19 Ce = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}e=1.602×10−19C in course calculations. A positive net charge usually indicates an electron deficit. A negative net charge indicates excess electrons. Ordinary rubbing transfers electrons rather than creating charge.

Quantization, conservation, and charging mechanisms

q=(Np−Ne)e,N=∣q∣e,Δm=Nme.q=(N_p-N_e)e,\quad N=\frac{|q|}{e},\quad \Delta m=N m_e.q=(Np​−Ne​)e,N=e∣q∣​,Δm=Nme​.

For ordinary isolated charged bodies, q is an integer multiple of e. An isolated system conserves total signed charge: ∑qbefore=∑qafter\sum q_{\mathrm{before}} = \sum q_{\mathrm{after}}∑qbefore​=∑qafter​. Neutral means balanced net charge, not absence of charged particles. Charge is frame invariant in the classical situations covered here.

Worked example — primary p. 8. A charge of +0.32 C+ 0.32\,\mathrm{C}+0.32C represents 0.32(1.602×10−19)=1.998×1018\frac{0.32}{\left( 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \right)} = 1.998 \times 10^{18}(1.602×10−19)0.32​=1.998×1018 removed electrons. Its mass decreases by about 1.82×10−12 kg1.82 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}1.82×10−12kg if only electron transfer changes its mass. Neutrino oscillations show that neutrinos are not all massless. The source's blanket zero-rest-mass statement is inaccurate and unnecessary for this charge calculation.

Conduction requires contact and permits charge transfer. Friction transfers charge during rubbing. Induction separates charge without contact with the inducing body. To leave a single conductor with net charge by the standard grounding method, approach the charged rod, connect the ground, remove the ground, then remove the rod. Changing that order can remove the intended final charge. Polarization separates positive and negative charge slightly within a neutral object; attraction does not prove the object has acquired a net charge.

Conductors have mobile charges. Insulators restrict bulk charge motion. Semiconductors have conductivity between these broad categories and strongly depend on material conditions. In electrostatic equilibrium, excess conductor charge lies on its surface; the field inside conducting material is zero. These statements concern equilibrium, not every current-carrying wire.

Coulomb's law: empirical starting law and algebraic forms

For stationary point charges in vacuum, use k≈8.99×109 N⋅m2C2k \approx \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{N} \cdot m^{2}}{C^{2}}k≈C28.99×109N⋅m2​. Coulomb's inverse-square law is an empirical starting law here; it cannot be independently proved just by rearranging its definition.

F=k∣q1q2∣r2,r=k∣q1q2∣F,∣q1∣=Fr2k∣q2∣.F=k\frac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2},\quad r=\sqrt{\frac{k|q_1q_2|}{F}},\quad |q_1|=\frac{Fr^2}{k|q_2|}.F=kr2∣q1​q2​∣​,r=Fk∣q1​q2​∣​​,∣q1​∣=k∣q2​∣Fr2​.

Use magnitudes in this scalar formula. Determine attraction or repulsion separately. Like signs repel; opposite signs attract. Doubling r divides F by four. Tripling one charge triples F. In a uniform linear medium with relative permittivity κ\kappaκ, replace ε0\varepsilon_{0}ε0​ by κε0\kappa \varepsilon_{0}κε0​ if the problem justifies that model.

Worked example — primary p. 22. q1=+25 nCq_{1} = + 25\,\mathrm{nC}q1​=+25nC, q2=−75 nCq_{2} = - 75\,\mathrm{nC}q2​=−75nC, r=3.0 cm=0.030 mr = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.030\,\mathrm{m}r=3.0cm=0.030m. F=(8.99×109)(25×10−9)(75×10−9)(0.030)2=0.01873 N\begin{aligned}F &= \frac{\left( 8.99 \times 10^{9} \right) \left( 25 \times 10^{-9} \right) \left( 75 \times 10^{-9} \right)}{\left( 0.030 \right)^{2}} \\&= 0.01873\,\mathrm{N}\end{aligned}F​=(0.030)2(8.99×109)(25×10−9)(75×10−9)​=0.01873N​ Both forces have this magnitude. Their directions are opposite and attractive. A larger charge does not experience the larger force in this two-body pair.

Superposition in one, two, and three dimensions

Define the displacement from source j to the target i as ri − rj. This definition prevents ambiguous subscript conventions:

Fi=∑j≠ikqiqjri−rj∣ri−rj∣3.\mathbf F_i=\sum_{j\ne i} kq_iq_j\frac{\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j|^3}.Fi​=j=i∑​kqi​qj​∣ri​−rj​∣3ri​−rj​​.

Derive the component form. A unit displacement vector is Δrr\frac{\Delta r}{r}rΔr​. Multiplying it by kqiqjr2\frac{kq_{i} q_{j}}{r^{2}}r2kqi​qj​​ gives the denominator r3r^{3}r3. Therefore Fi,x=∑j≠ikqiqj(xi−xj)∣ri−rj∣3F_{i,x}=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{kq_iq_j(x_i-x_j)}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_j|^3}Fi,x​=∑j=i​∣ri​−rj​∣3kqi​qj​(xi​−xj​)​, with analogous y and z terms. Combine components before computing magnitude:

F=Fx2+Fy2+Fz2,θ=atan2⁡(Fy,Fx).F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2+F_z^2},\quad \theta=\operatorname{atan2}(F_y,F_x).F=Fx2​+Fy2​+Fz2​​,θ=atan2(Fy​,Fx​).

Ordinary tan⁡−1(FyFx)\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{F_{y}}{F_{x}} \right)tan−1(Fx​Fy​​) needs a quadrant check. Forces on different targets cannot be added to answer “net force on q1q_{1}q1​.” Exclude the target's own field.

Worked example — primary pp. 24–25. A +5 nC+ 5\,\mathrm{nC}+5nC target is at x=0x = 0x=0. A +1 nC+ 1\,\mathrm{nC}+1nC source at +0.020 m+ 0.020\,\mathrm{m}+0.020m repels it left with 112.375 μN112.375\,\mathrm{\mu N}112.375μN. A −3 nC- 3\,\mathrm{nC}−3nC source at +0.040 m+ 0.040\,\mathrm{m}+0.040m attracts it right with 84.281 μN84.281\,\mathrm{\mu N}84.281μN. Fx=−112.375+84.281=−28.094 μNF_{x} = - 112.375 + 84.281 = - 28.094\,\mathrm{\mu N}Fx​=−112.375+84.281=−28.094μN. Thus the net force is about 28 μN28\,\mathrm{\mu N}28μN left. Adding the magnitudes would be wrong.

Rectangles, diagonals, and force cancellation

For the rectangular arrangement in primary pp. 26–28, draw all forces on the SAME corner charge. A 3–4–5 rectangle has diagonal r=5r = 5r=5 units. A diagonal force's component factors are 45\frac{4}{5}54​ and 35\frac{3}{5}53​ when the horizontal side is 4 units. The diagonal force is 230.4 μN230.4\,\mathrm{\mu N}230.4μN with k=9×109k = 9 \times 10^{9}k=9×109. Its magnitude does not decide its component signs. The complete solution below corrects the previous factor-of-ten error in these notes.

The source's working mixes a downward −90° direction with a positive j term. Recompute from the arrows instead of copying that sign. If a diagonal force points upper-left, its components are (−4F5- \frac{4 F}{5}−54F​, +3F5+ \frac{3 F}{5}+53F​). Add the horizontal and vertical forces algebraically after resolving the diagonal.

For two like-signed sources on a line, a cancellation point lies between them. For opposite signs, their fields reinforce between them; a possible zero-field point lies outside on the smaller-magnitude charge's side. Solve in each physically allowed region. Squaring distance equations can produce an invalid location.

Derive the cancellation location. Put positive Q1Q_{1}Q1​ at x=0x = 0x=0 and positive Q2Q_{2}Q2​ at x=dx = dx=d. A nonzero test charge between them has opposing forces. Cancel its magnitude and k: Q1x2=Q2(d−x)2\frac{Q_{1}}{x^{2}} = \frac{Q_{2}}{\left( d - x \right)^{2}}x2Q1​​=(d−x)2Q2​​. Both distances are positive in this region. Taking positive square roots and collecting x gives:

Q1(d−x)=Q2x⇒x=dQ1Q1+Q2.\sqrt{Q_1}(d-x)=\sqrt{Q_2}x\Rightarrow x=\frac{d\sqrt{Q_1}}{\sqrt{Q_1}+\sqrt{Q_2}}.Q1​​(d−x)=Q2​​x⇒x=Q1​​+Q2​​dQ1​​​.

For +4 nC+ 4\,\mathrm{nC}+4nC and +9 nC+ 9\,\mathrm{nC}+9nC separated by 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m, x=2(2+3)=0.400 mx = \frac{2}{\left( 2 + 3 \right)} = 0.400\,\mathrm{m}x=(2+3)2​=0.400m from +4 nC+ 4\,\mathrm{nC}+4nC. The fields there have equal magnitudes and opposite directions. The point is closer to the smaller charge because its weaker source needs a smaller distance to match the other field.

Substitution gives equal field magnitudes 8.99 NC8.99\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}8.99CN​, with opposite directions. Equal opposite charges have no finite zero-field point on their joining line.

For a proton and electron separated by 5.3×10−11 m5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m}5.3×10−11m, Fe≈8.21×10−8 NF_{e} \approx 8.21 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{N}Fe​≈8.21×10−8N and Fg≈3.62×10−47 NF_{g} \approx 3.62 \times 10^{-47}\,\mathrm{N}Fg​≈3.62×10−47N. Their ratio is ke2(Gmemp)\frac{ke^{2}}{\left( Gm_{e} m_{p} \right)}(Gme​mp​)ke2​, independent of r. Both forces attract, but they are not comparable in size. Source problems · full working

Charging diagrams and charge-conservation calculations

Names and signs — primary pp. 4–6. The historical word “electric” comes from the Greek word for amber. The coulomb names the charge unit after Coulomb. Franklin's positive and negative labels distinguish the two charge signs. “Positive” does not mean more electrons; an electron deficit gives a positive net charge in the ordinary charging examples.

Particle Approximate mass, kg Charge, C
Electron 9.11×10−319.11 \times 10^{-31}9.11×10−31 −1.602×10−19- 1.602 \times 10^{-19}−1.602×10−19
Proton 1.673×10−271.673 \times 10^{-27}1.673×10−27 +1.602×10−19+ 1.602 \times 10^{-19}+1.602×10−19
Neutron 1.675×10−271.675 \times 10^{-27}1.675×10−27 0

Source correction. Primary p. 21 repeats the proton's mass for the neutron. Their masses are close but not identical. The rounded values above distinguish them. A neutral object can contain many charged particles; their net charge cancels.

Grounding. Earth acts as a large charge reservoir. Connecting a conductor to ground lets electrons move as the surrounding electric field requires. With a nearby negative rod, electrons leave the grounded conductor. Remove the ground first, then the rod: the conductor remains positive. A positive inducing rod draws electrons from ground and leaves the conductor negative after the same removal sequence.

Conduction versus polarization. A charged metal redistributes mobile electrons over its surface. Charge on an insulating rod does not spread as freely. Neutral paper can still be attracted to a charged comb. Polarization places the nearer opposite-sign charge slightly closer, making its attraction exceed the farther like-sign repulsion. Attraction alone does not prove a net charge.

Identical conducting spheres share charge equally: a labeled extension

For two isolated identical metal spheres that touch, conservation gives Qtotal=Q1+Q2Q_{\mathrm{total}} = Q_{1} + Q_{2}Qtotal​=Q1​+Q2​. Symmetry gives equal final charges after they reach equilibrium. Therefore Qfinal,each=Q1+Q22Q_{\mathrm{final,each}}=\frac{Q_1+Q_2}{2}Qfinal,each​=2Q1​+Q2​​.

For +8 nC+ 8\,\mathrm{nC}+8nC and −2 nC- 2\,\mathrm{nC}−2nC, the total is +6 nC+ 6\,\mathrm{nC}+6nC, so each ends with +3 nC+ 3\,\mathrm{nC}+3nC. The initially negative sphere loses enough electrons to become positive. Unequal spheres do not generally share charge equally. Widely separated spherical conductors have equal potentials at equilibrium, giving approximately Q1R1=Q2R2\frac{Q_{1}}{R_{1}} = \frac{Q_{2}}{R_{2}}R1​Q1​​=R2​Q2​​ before disconnection in that ideal model.

Module 04 / Physics 2

Electric fields: calculate the field before inserting a test charge

Field directions, superposition, motion, and continuous distributions.

Topics in this module
Derive the point-charge field and its inverse formsField lines, dipoles, and equipattern reasoningDiscrete-source superposition and a midpoint exampleUniform-field motion: derive the trajectoryContinuous charge distributions: a labeled extensionRead field diagrams and solve the primary examples completelyDerive the companion's three-charge field and the dipole limitsMotion problems: initial conditions, stopping, and deflection

An electric field assigns a force-per-charge vector to each point. It is not merely an area with electricity. A source charge produces its field even when no test particle is present. Define field direction by the force on a positive test charge.

E=Fq0,F=q0E,[E]=N/C=V/m.\mathbf E=\frac{\mathbf F}{q_0},\quad \mathbf F=q_0\mathbf E,\quad [E]=\mathrm{N/C}=\mathrm{V/m}.E=q0​F​,F=q0​E,[E]=N/C=V/m.

For a negative test charge, force opposes E. The source charge sets the field; the test charge sets the force experienced in that field. The ideal test charge is small enough not to rearrange the source distribution significantly.

Derive the point-charge field and its inverse forms

Substitute Coulomb's force into E=Fq0E = \frac{F}{q_{0}}E=q0​F​ and cancel the positive test-charge magnitude:

E=k∣Q∣r2,∣Q∣=Er2k,r=k∣Q∣E.E=\frac{k|Q|}{r^2},\quad |Q|=\frac{Er^2}{k},\quad r=\sqrt{\frac{k|Q|}{E}}.E=r2k∣Q∣​,∣Q∣=kEr2​,r=Ek∣Q∣​​.

E points away from positive Q and toward negative Q. The field magnitude decreases as 1r2\frac{1}{r^{2}}r21​. The value at r=0r = 0r=0 is not finite in the point-charge idealization.

Worked example — primary p. 12. A +3.0×10−8 C+ 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}+3.0×10−8C test charge experiences 6.0×10−8 N6.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{N}6.0×10−8N. E=2.0 NCE = 2.0\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}E=2.0CN​. Replacing it with +12×10−8 C+ 12 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}+12×10−8C gives F=2.4×10−7 NF = 2.4 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{N}F=2.4×10−7N in the same direction. Replacing it with a negative charge reverses the force, not the pre-existing field.

Worked examples — primary pp. 29–30. A +4.0 nC+ 4.0\,\mathrm{nC}+4.0nC source gives E=9.0 NCE = 9.0\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}E=9.0CN​ at 2.0 m2.0\,\mathrm{m}2.0m when k=9.0×109k = 9.0 \times 10^{9}k=9.0×109. Conversely, E=5 NCE = 5\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}E=5CN​ at 1.50 m1.50\,\mathrm{m}1.50m requires ∣Q∣=1.25×10−9 C\left| Q \right| = 1.25 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{C}∣Q∣=1.25×10−9C. Magnitude alone does not identify the source's sign.

Field lines, dipoles, and equipattern reasoning

The tangent to a field line gives the local field direction. Denser lines indicate stronger field. Lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges or at infinity. Line counts communicate relative magnitude; they are not physical wires. Electrostatic field lines do not cross because the field has one direction at a regular point.

A dipole has equal and opposite separated charges. Equal like charges can cancel at their midpoint. Equal opposite charges do not cancel their midpoint fields: both point from positive to negative. A curved field line is not generally a charged particle's trajectory; motion also depends on initial velocity and inertia.

E(r)=k∑jQjr−rj∣r−rj∣3.\mathbf E(\mathbf r)=k\sum_j Q_j\frac{\mathbf r-\mathbf r_j}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_j|^3}.E(r)=kj∑​Qj​∣r−rj​∣3r−rj​​.

Thus Ex=kq[1x2+2x(x2+a2)3/2]E_{x} = kq \left[ \frac{1}{x^{2}} + \frac{2 x}{\left( x^{2} + a^{2} \right)^{3/2}} \right]Ex​=kq[x21​+(x2+a2)3/22x​], Ey=0E_{y} = 0Ey​=0. Uniform-field motion: derive the trajectory

Combine Newton's law ma=qEma = qEma=qE with constant-acceleration kinematics. For a constant field along y:

ay=qEym,x=x0+v0xt,y=y0+v0yt+qEy2mt2.a_y=\frac{qE_y}{m},\quad x=x_0+v_{0x}t,\quad y=y_0+v_{0y}t+\frac{qE_y}{2m}t^2.ay​=mqEy​​,x=x0​+v0x​t,y=y0​+v0y​t+2mqEy​​t2.

When v0x≠0v_{0x} \ne 0v0x​=0, eliminate t=(x−x0)v0xt = \frac{\left( x - x_{0} \right)}{v_{0}} xt=v0​(x−x0​)​x. The resulting y(x) is parabolic. An electron has q=−eq = - eq=−e; do not substitute +e for its acceleration. A particle initially moving along E can speed up or slow down depending on q and its velocity direction.

Worked example. An electron enters horizontally at 2.0×106 ms2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}2.0×106sm​ through a 0.020 m0.020\,\mathrm{m}0.020m long uniform-field region. Source problems · full working

Read field diagrams and solve the primary examples completely

Source and field points. A source point identifies the charge producing the field. A field point identifies where E is evaluated. The field equation uses their separation, not the source's distance from an arbitrary coordinate origin.

Field-line diagnosis — primary p. 20. Reject crossing electrostatic lines. Check that lines leave positive charges and enter negative charges. Check that line counts reflect relative charge magnitudes. Check that stronger fields have closer line spacing. Do not treat the number of lines as an independently measurable number of physical threads.

Worked solution↳

Field from a measured test-charge force

Source: Primary p. 12. Given: q0=+3.0×10−8 Cq_{0} = + 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}q0​=+3.0×10−8C and F0=6.0×10−8 NF_{0} = 6.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{N}F0​=6.0×10−8N.

  2. Preserve the force direction as the field direction because q0q_{0}q0​ is positive.
  3. Replace the charge with +12×10−8 C+ 12 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}+12×10−8C while keeping the source distribution fixed.
  4. Calculate Fnew=qnewE=(12×10−8)(2.0)=2.4×10−7 N\begin{aligned}F_{\mathrm{new}} &= q_{\mathrm{new}}E \\&= \left( 12 \times 10^{-8} \right) \left( 2.0 \right) \\&= 2.4 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{N}\end{aligned}Fnew​​=qnew​E=(12×10−8)(2.0)=2.4×10−7N​

Check. The test charge increases fourfold, so its force increases fourfold. E does not change in the ideal non-disturbing-test-charge model.

Derive the companion's three-charge field and the dipole limits

Derivation∴

Three equal charges on the y-axis

Source: Companion p. 2. Put equal charges q at (0,d), (0,0), and (0,−d). Evaluate at (x,0), with x>0x > 0x>0.

  1. Find the outer distances r=(x2+d2)r = \sqrt{\left( x^{2} + d^{2} \right)}r=(x2+d2)​. The central distance is x.
  2. Use Coulomb's field magnitude k∣q∣r2\frac{k \left| q \right|}{r^{2}}r2k∣q∣​ for either outer source.
  3. Project horizontally with cos⁡θ=xr\cos \theta = \frac{x}{r}cosθ=rx​. Each outer x component is kqxr3\frac{kqx}{r^{3}}r3kqx​.
  4. Cancel the equal, opposite y components.
  5. Add the central x component kqx2\frac{kq}{x^{2}}x2kq​ and both outer x components.
Ex=kqx2+2kqx2+d2xx2+d2=kq[1x2+2x(x2+d2)3/2],Ey=0.\begin{aligned} E_x&=\frac{kq}{x^2}+2\frac{kq}{x^2+d^2}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+d^2}}\\ &=kq\left[\frac1{x^2}+\frac{2x}{(x^2+d^2)^{3/2}}\right], \qquad E_y=0. \end{aligned}Ex​​=x2kq​+2x2+d2kq​x2+d2​x​=kq[x21​+(x2+d2)3/22x​],Ey​=0.​

Limit check. Far away, x ≫ d, the result tends to 3kqx2\frac{3 kq}{x^{2}}x23kq​. The collection then resembles one point charge of total charge 3q. At x → 0, the central point-charge term diverges; do not substitute x=0x = 0x=0 into the formula.

Derivation∴

Electric dipole: axial and perpendicular-bisector fields, labeled extensions

Put −q at x=−ax = - ax=−a and +q at x=+ax = + ax=+a. The dipole moment has magnitude p=2aqp = 2 aqp=2aq and points from negative to positive.

For an axial point x>ax > ax>a, the two fields oppose. Subtract their signed x components:

Eaxis=kq[1(x−a)2−1(x+a)2]=4kqax(x2−a2)2⟶2kpx3(x≫a).\begin{gathered}E_{axis}=kq\left[\frac1{(x-a)^2}-\frac1{(x+a)^2}\right] =\frac{4kqax}{(x^2-a^2)^2} \longrightarrow\frac{2kp}{x^3}\\(x\gg a).\end{gathered}Eaxis​=kq[(x−a)21​−(x+a)21​]=(x2−a2)24kqax​⟶x32kp​(x≫a).​

For a point (0,y) on the perpendicular bisector, both source distances equal (a2+y2)\sqrt{\left( a^{2} + y^{2} \right)}(a2+y2)​. The y components cancel. The x components both point toward −x:

Ex=−2kqa(a2+y2)3/2=−kp(a2+y2)3/2,Ey=0.E_x=-\frac{2kqa}{(a^2+y^2)^{3/2}} =-\frac{kp}{(a^2+y^2)^{3/2}},\qquad E_y=0.Ex​=−(a2+y2)3/22kqa​=−(a2+y2)3/2kp​,Ey​=0.

Far away on that bisector, the magnitude tends to kp∣y∣3\frac{kp}{\left| y \right|^{3}}∣y∣3kp​. Compare the dipole's 1r3\frac{1}{r^{3}}r31​ far field with a nonzero net point charge's 1r2\frac{1}{r^{2}}r21​ field. These extensions explain the dipole patterns shown in both decks.

Motion problems: initial conditions, stopping, and deflection

Derivation∴

Derive the stopping distance in a uniform electric field

This is a labeled extension of primary pp. 24–25. Let a positive charge enter along +x while E points along −x. Neglect other forces.

  1. Write ax=−qEma_{x} = - \frac{qE}{m}ax​=−mqE​, where E denotes the positive field magnitude.
  2. Use vx=v0v_{x} = v_{0}vx​=v0​+at. Setting vx=0v_{x} = 0vx​=0 gives tstop=mv0(qE)t_{\mathrm{stop}} = \frac{mv_{0}}{\left( qE \right)}tstop​=(qE)mv0​​.
  3. Use vx2=v02+2aΔxv_{x}^{2} = v_{0}^{2} + 2 a\Delta xvx2​=v02​+2aΔx. Set vx=0v_{x} = 0vx​=0 and isolate the stopping distance.
dstop=mv022qE.d_{stop}=\frac{mv_0^2}{2qE}.dstop​=2qEmv02​​.

The particle reaches a turning point only if the uniform-field region extends that far. After stopping, the force still acts, so the particle reverses direction. Zero instantaneous velocity does not mean zero acceleration.

Extension of the uniform-field diagrams. Let an electron enter horizontally at 2.0×106 ms2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}2.0×106sm​. The field region is 0.020 m0.020\,\mathrm{m}0.020m long, with Ey=+100 NCE_{y} = + 100\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}Ey​=+100CN​.   3. Find exit displacement y=12ayt2≈−8.793×10−4 my = \tfrac{1}{2} a_{y} t^{2} \approx - 8.793 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}y=21​ay​t2≈−8.793×10−4m, or −0.8793 mm- 0.8793\,\mathrm{mm}−0.8793mm.

Why the path curves downward. The field points upward, but the electron is negative. Its horizontal speed stays constant only because this model has no horizontal force.

Module 05 / Physics 2

Electric potential: scalar sums, signed energy

Work, signed potential energy, potential, and equipotential surfaces.

Topics in this module
Work, energy, and consistent endpoint labelsDerive point-charge potential from fieldPair energy and assembling several chargesField–potential relation and equipotentialsSpeed from a potential changeExtensions: uniform rings and finite rodsWork signs, coordinate choices, and the battery modelComplete the symbolic charge-assembly examplesComplete the companion potential and dipole problems

Electric potential V is energy per charge. Potential energy U belongs to a charge configuration. One volt is one joule per coulomb. A point can have nonzero V and zero E; a zero potential does not imply zero field.

Work, energy, and consistent endpoint labels

For a constant force, W=Fdcos⁡θW = Fd \cos \thetaW=Fdcosθ. More generally W=∫F⋅dlW = \int F \cdot dlW=∫F⋅dl. The net-work theorem is Wnet=ΔKW_{\mathrm{net}} = \Delta KWnet​=ΔK. For the electrostatic force, Wfield=−ΔUW_{\mathrm{field}} = - \Delta UWfield​=−ΔU. A slow external mover with no kinetic-energy change does Wexternal=+ΔUW_{\mathrm{external}} = + \Delta UWexternal​=+ΔU. The external-work equality requires those conditions; it is not true for arbitrary accelerated motion.

ΔU=q(Vb−Va),Wfield=q(Va−Vb),ΔK=−qΔV.\Delta U=q(V_b-V_a),\quad W_{field}=q(V_a-V_b),\quad \Delta K=-q\Delta V.ΔU=q(Vb​−Va​),Wfield​=q(Va​−Vb​),ΔK=−qΔV.

The ΔK\Delta KΔK expression assumes that the electrostatic force supplies all the net work. Include other forces separately when they do work. Some slides define Vab=Va−VbV_{ab} = V_{a} - V_{b}Vab​=Va​−Vb​. These notes define ΔV=Vb−Va\Delta V = V_{b} - V_{a}ΔV=Vb​−Va​ when discussing a move a → b. Write the endpoint order before substituting. The primary's statement that work equals voltage omits division by charge: work PER charge equals an appropriate potential difference.

Worked example. A +2 μC+ 2\,\mathrm{\mu C}+2μC charge moves from 100 V100\,\mathrm{V}100V to 40 V40\,\mathrm{V}40V. ΔV=−60 V\Delta V = - 60\,\mathrm{V}ΔV=−60V, ΔU=−120 μJ\Delta U = - 120\,\mathrm{\mu J}ΔU=−120μJ, and Wfield=+120 μJW_{\mathrm{field}} = + 120\,\mathrm{\mu J}Wfield​=+120μJ. For −2 μC- 2\,\mathrm{\mu C}−2μC over the same endpoints, the energy and work signs reverse. The field direction still points toward decreasing potential.

Derive point-charge potential from field

Choose V(∞)=0V \left( \infty \right) = 0V(∞)=0 for an isolated source. Integrate the radial electric field:

V(r)−V(∞)=−∫∞rkQs2 ds=kQr.V(r)-V(\infty)=-\int_\infty^r\frac{kQ}{s^2}\,ds=\frac{kQ}{r}.V(r)−V(∞)=−∫∞r​s2kQ​ds=rkQ​.

Keep the sign of Q. Rearrange to Q=VrkQ = \frac{Vr}{k}Q=kVr​ or r=kQVr = \frac{kQ}{V}r=VkQ​ when the signs produce a positive r. A zero-V denominator cannot locate a finite nonzero-charge equipotential. For multiple fixed sources, V=k∑iQiriV=k\sum_i\frac{Q_i}{r_i}V=k∑i​ri​Qi​​. Add scalar signed contributions, not vector components.

Worked example — primary p. 34. At 0.50 m0.50\,\mathrm{m}0.50m from ±20 μC20\,\mathrm{\mu C}20μC, V=±3.6×105 VV = \pm 3.6 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{V}V=±3.6×105V with k=9×109k = 9 \times 10^{9}k=9×109. The distance is positive in both cases. The source charge determines the sign.

Worked example — primary p. 35. q1=2 nCq_{1} = 2\,\mathrm{nC}q1​=2nC at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0); q2=6 nCq_{2} = 6\,\mathrm{nC}q2​=6nC at (0.06,0) m(0.06,0)\,\mathrm{m}(0.06,0)m. At A=(0,0.07) mA=(0,0.07)\,\mathrm{m}A=(0,0.07)m, r1=0.07 mr_{1} = 0.07\,\mathrm{m}r1​=0.07m and r2=(0.062+0.072)=0.092195 mr_{2} = \sqrt{\left( 0.06^{2} + 0.07^{2} \right)} = 0.092195\,\mathrm{m}r2​=(0.062+0.072)​=0.092195m. VA=9×109[2×10−90.07+6×10−90.092195]≈842.86 VV_{A} = 9 \times 10^{9} \left[ \frac{2 \times 10^{-9}}{0.07} + \frac{6 \times 10^{-9}}{0.092195} \right] \approx 842.86\,\mathrm{V}VA​=9×109[0.072×10−9​+0.0921956×10−9​]≈842.86V. Early rounding r2r_{2}r2​ to 0.092 m0.092\,\mathrm{m}0.092m gives about 844.10 V844.10\,\mathrm{V}844.10V, explaining the source's nearby rounded answer.

Pair energy and assembling several charges

Multiply source potential by the added test charge: U=qV=kQqrU = qV = \frac{kQq}{r}U=qV=rkQq​. Positive pair energy occurs for like charges with the infinity reference. Negative pair energy occurs for opposite charges. Negative energy is not a negative distance or an impossible state.

Derivation — assembly. Bring q1q_{1}q1​ from infinity first: no interaction work. Bring q2q_{2}q2​: add kq1q2r12\frac{kq_{1} q_{2}}{r_{12}}r12​kq1​q2​​. Bring q3q_{3}q3​: add kq3q1r13+kq3q2r23\frac{kq_{3} q_{1}}{r_{13}} + \frac{kq_{3} q_{2}}{r_{23}}r13​kq3​q1​​+r23​kq3​q2​​. Therefore:

Usystem=k∑i<jqiqjrij=12∑iqiVothers(ri).U_{system}=k\sum_{i<j}\frac{q_iq_j}{r_{ij}}=\frac12\sum_i q_i V_{others}(\mathbf r_i).Usystem​=ki<j∑​rij​qi​qj​​=21​i∑​qi​Vothers​(ri​).

The pair restriction prevents counting twice and excludes self-interaction. The factor 12\frac{1}{2}21​ is necessary only in the second expression, not in a direct list of unique pairs.

Worked example — primary p. 26. q1=+4 nCq_{1} = + 4\,\mathrm{nC}q1​=+4nC at 0, q2=−3 nCq_{2} = - 3\,\mathrm{nC}q2​=−3nC at 0.20 m0.20\,\mathrm{m}0.20m, q3=+2 nCq_{3} = + 2\,\mathrm{nC}q3​=+2nC at 0.10 m0.10\,\mathrm{m}0.10m. Distances are 0.20, 0.10, 0.10 m0.10\,\mathrm{m}0.10m. U=9×109[(−12×10−18)0.20+(8×10−18)0.10+(−6×10−18)0.10]=−3.60×10−7 J\begin{aligned}U &= 9 \times 10^{9} \left[ \frac{\left( - 12 \times 10^{-18} \right)}{0.20} + \frac{\left( 8 \times 10^{-18} \right)}{0.10} + \frac{\left( - 6 \times 10^{-18} \right)}{0.10} \right] \\&= - 3.60 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{J}\end{aligned}U​=9×109[0.20(−12×10−18)​+0.10(8×10−18)​+0.10(−6×10−18)​]=−3.60×10−7J​ Charge order on the line does not replace the need to calculate all pair distances.

For bringing a new charge q into an existing fixed-source arrangement, Wexternal=q[Vexisting(final)−Vexisting(initial)]W_{\mathrm{external}}=q\left[V_{\mathrm{existing}}(\mathrm{final})-V_{\mathrm{existing}}(\mathrm{initial})\right]Wexternal​=q[Vexisting​(final)−Vexisting​(initial)], provided the move is quasistatic. Do not re-add energy already stored among the fixed source charges.

Field–potential relation and equipotentials

ΔV=−∫abE⋅dl,E=−∇V.\Delta V=-\int_a^b\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l,\quad \mathbf E=-\nabla V.ΔV=−∫ab​E⋅dl,E=−∇V.

For uniform E, ΔV=−Edcos⁡θ\Delta V = - Ed \cos \thetaΔV=−Edcosθ where θ\thetaθ is the angle between E and displacement. If motion is parallel to an equipotential, ΔV=0\Delta V = 0ΔV=0, so electrostatic work is zero. Field lines are perpendicular to equipotential surfaces where E is nonzero. At a field-zero point, there is no unique local field direction to draw.

Worked example — primary pp. 39–40. For q=4 nCq = 4\,\mathrm{nC}q=4nC and k=9×109k = 9 \times 10^{9}k=9×109, kq=36 V⋅mkq = 36\,\mathrm{V} \cdot mkq=36V⋅m. The 10, 20, and 30 V30\,\mathrm{V}30V surfaces have radii 3.6, 1.8, and 1.2 m1.2\,\mathrm{m}1.2m. They are spheres; a plane through the charge shows circles. Equal voltage intervals do not give equal radial intervals.

Speed from a potential change

Combine conservation of energy with K=mv22K = \frac{mv^{2}}{2}K=2mv2​:

vf=vi2−2qΔVm.v_f=\sqrt{v_i^2-\frac{2q\Delta V}{m}}.vf​=vi2​−m2qΔV​​.

The expression inside the root must be nonnegative. A negative value means the particle cannot reach that endpoint with the stated initial energy. From rest, an electron accelerates through a positive potential increase; a positive particle accelerates toward lower potential.

Companion example, p. 3. A proton moves from rest 0.20 m0.20\,\mathrm{m}0.20m along E=1.0×103 NCE = 1.0 \times 10^{3}\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}E=1.0×103CN​. Use the slide'sqp=1.60×10−19 Cs q_{p} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}sqp​=1.60×10−19C and mp=1.67×10−27 kgm_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}mp​=1.67×10−27kg. Wfield=qpEd=3.20×10−17 JW_{\mathrm{field}} = q_{p} Ed = 3.20 \times 10^{-17}\,\mathrm{J}Wfield​=qp​Ed=3.20×10−17J. Therefore v=(2Wmp)≈1.96×105 msv = \sqrt{\left( \frac{2 W}{m_{p}} \right)} \approx 1.96 \times 10^{5}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}v=(mp​2W​)​≈1.96×105sm​. The potential change is −200 V- 200\,\mathrm{V}−200V. The previous notes used a different field value; this solution now matches the supplied slide.

Extensions: uniform rings and finite rods

Potential often simplifies a symmetric field calculation. On a ring's axis, every element has the same distance, giving V=kQ(x2+R2)V = \frac{kQ}{\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + R^{2} \right)}}V=(x2+R2)​kQ​. Differentiating −dVdx- \frac{dV}{dx}−dxdV​ gives the ring field in M4. At the ring center, V=kQRV = \frac{kQ}{R}V=RkQ​ while E=0E = 0E=0.

For a uniform rod from x=ax = ax=a to b and a field point on the same axis outside the rod, integrate dV=kλdxdV = k\lambda dxdV=kλdx/distance. The integral contains a logarithm, not the inverse-square antiderivative used for a point field. Set positive distances and the reference explicitly. These integrations are extensions of superposition, not replacements for the source's point-charge examples.

Complete the rod integration. Put the field point at x=s>bx = s > bx=s>b, with λ\lambdaλ constant and V(∞)=0V \left( \infty \right) = 0V(∞)=0. Each element's distance is s−x. The integration gives:

V(s)=kλ∫abdxs−x=kλln⁡s−as−b,Ex=−dVds=kλ(1s−b−1s−a).\begin{gathered}V(s)=k\lambda\int_a^b\frac{dx}{s-x}=k\lambda\ln\frac{s-a}{s-b},\\E_x=-\frac{dV}{ds}=k\lambda\left(\frac1{s-b}-\frac1{s-a}\right).\end{gathered}V(s)=kλ∫ab​s−xdx​=kλlns−bs−a​,Ex​=−dsdV​=kλ(s−b1​−s−a1​).​

For a=0a = 0a=0, b=0.20 mb = 0.20\,\mathrm{m}b=0.20m, s=0.50 ms = 0.50\,\mathrm{m}s=0.50m, and λ=2.0 nCm\lambda = \frac{2.0\,\mathrm{nC}}{m}λ=m2.0nC​, V≈9.18465 VV \approx 9.18465\,\mathrm{V}V≈9.18465V and Ex≈23.9733 NCE_{x} \approx 23.9733\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}Ex​≈23.9733CN​. The logarithm uses a dimensionless ratio. The positive field points away from the positive rod.

Work signs, coordinate choices, and the battery model

The companion'sU=qEss U = qEssU=qEs uses a position coordinate s measured opposite to its leftward field. It is not a direction-free rule. With +x along a uniform field, V(x)=V(0)−ExV \left( x \right) = V \left( 0 \right) - E_{x}V(x)=V(0)−Ex​ and U(x)=U(0)−qExU \left( x \right) = U \left( 0 \right) - qE_{x}U(x)=U(0)−qEx​. The reference constant does not affect a force or energy difference.

Displacement Charge sign ΔV\Delta VΔV ΔU=qΔV\Delta U = q\Delta VΔU=qΔV Wfield=−ΔUW_{\mathrm{field}} = - \Delta UWfield​=−ΔU
Along E Positive Negative Negative Positive
Along E Negative Negative Positive Negative
Against E Positive Positive Positive Negative
Against E Negative Positive Negative Positive

The table describes the electrostatic work during a specified displacement. It does not say that every particle initially moves in its force direction. A particle can initially move against its force and slow down.

Battery model — primary pp. 30–31; companion p. 6. Chemical processes move charge through the source against electrostatic forces. The supplied energy per positive charge is the emf, E=Wchemicalq\mathcal{E} = \frac{W_{\mathrm{chemical}}}{q}E=qWchemical​​. An ideal DC battery maintains a fixed terminal voltage. A real battery's terminal voltage depends on current and internal resistance. A generator can produce a changing voltage, so “all electrical sources supply a constant potential difference” is too broad.

External work to bring +e to x=2ax = 2 ax=2a

Source: Primary p. 17. Fixed charges are −e at x=0x = 0x=0 and +e at x=ax = ax=a. Bring a third +e from infinity to x=2ax = 2 ax=2a quasistatically.

  1. Find its final distances from the sources: 2a and a.
  2. Add the existing-source potentials at the destination: Vexisting=k(−e(2a)+ea)V_{\mathrm{existing}} = k \left( - \frac{e}{\left( 2 a \right)} + \frac{e}{a} \right)Vexisting​=k(−(2a)e​+ae​).

  4. Multiply by the added charge and use Vexisting(∞)=0V_{\mathrm{existing}} \left( \infty \right) = 0Vexisting​(∞)=0.
Wexternal=q3ΔVexisting=e(ke2a−0)=ke22a.W_{external}=q_3\Delta V_{existing} =e\left(\frac{ke}{2a}-0\right) =\frac{ke^2}{2a}.Wexternal​=q3​ΔVexisting​=e(2ake​−0)=2ake2​.

The electric field does the opposite work, −ke2(2a)- \frac{ke^{2}}{\left( 2 a \right)}−(2a)ke2​. Do not include the unchanged interaction energy between the first two charges in this work difference.

Total energy of the final three-charge configuration

Source: Primary p. 25. Use the same final positions: −e at 0, +e at a, and +e at 2a.

  1. List each unique pair once: (1,2), (1,3), and (2,3).
  2. Use distances a, 2a, and a respectively.
  3. Retain each product's sign before adding.
U12=−ke2a,U13=−ke22a,U23=+ke2a,Utotal=U12+U13+U23=−ke22a.\begin{aligned} U_{12}&=-\frac{ke^2}{a},& U_{13}&=-\frac{ke^2}{2a},& U_{23}&=+\frac{ke^2}{a},\\ U_{total}&=U_{12}+U_{13}+U_{23} =-\frac{ke^2}{2a}. \end{aligned}U12​Utotal​​=−ake2​,=U12​+U13​+U23​=−2ake2​.​U13​=−2ake2​,U23​=+ake2​,

The final total remains negative, −ke2(2a)- \frac{ke^{2}}{\left( 2 a \right)}−(2a)ke2​. Total configuration energy and work for one assembly stage answer different questions.

Va=108(10.060−10.040)=−900 V,Vb=108(10.040−10.140)=1928.57 V,Vc=108(10.130−10.130)=0.\begin{aligned} V_a&=108\left(\frac1{0.060}-\frac1{0.040}\right)=-900\ \mathrm V,\\ V_b&=108\left(\frac1{0.040}-\frac1{0.140}\right)=1928.57\ \mathrm V,\\ V_c&=108\left(\frac1{0.130}-\frac1{0.130}\right)=0. \end{aligned}Va​Vb​Vc​​=108(0.0601​−0.0401​)=−900 V,=108(0.0401​−0.1401​)=1928.57 V,=108(0.1301​−0.1301​)=0.​

Derivation∴

Derive why equipotentials are perpendicular to E

For an infinitesimal displacement dl along an equipotential, dV=0dV = 0dV=0. The electrostatic relation gives dV=−E⋅dldV = - E \cdot dldV=−E⋅dl. Therefore E⋅dl=0E \cdot dl = 0E⋅dl=0 for every tangent displacement. Where E is nonzero, E has no tangent component and must point normal to the surface.

For closely spaced equal-voltage contours, ∣E∣≈∣ΔV∣Δsnormal\left| E \right| \approx \frac{\left| \Delta V \right|}{\Delta s_{\mathrm{normal}}}∣E∣≈Δsnormal​∣ΔV∣​. Smaller normal spacing means a stronger field. Use perpendicular spacing, not an arbitrary diagonal separation between two contour points.

Module 06 / Physics 2

Capacitors: first decide what stays fixed

Plate geometry, dielectrics, charge, energy, and complete networks.

Topics in this module
Derive parallel-plate capacitanceDielectrics: connected versus disconnected batteryDerive all three energy expressionsNetworks: derive series and parallel rulesDerive capacitance with the charge, geometry, and units visibleRestore every capacitor in the source networksEnergy, dielectric insertion, and capacitor applications

A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between conductors. Its plates carry +Q and −Q. In C=QVC = \frac{Q}{V}C=VQ​, Q is the magnitude on ONE plate, not the algebraic total charge of the pair. One farad is one coulomb per volt. Use μF=10−6 F\mathrm{\mu F} = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}μF=10−6F, nF=10−9 F\mathrm{nF} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F}nF=10−9F, and pF=10−12 F\mathrm{pF} = 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F}pF=10−12F.

C=Q/V,Q=CV,V=Q/C.C=Q/V,\quad Q=CV,\quad V=Q/C.C=Q/V,Q=CV,V=Q/C.

For a linear ideal capacitor, geometry and dielectric determine C. A larger Q does not automatically mean a larger C: the applied voltage can increase in the same proportion. Capacitive keyboard keys exploit smaller separation increasing capacitance.

Derive parallel-plate capacitance

For large parallel plates with edge effects neglected, σ=QA\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}σ=AQ​ and E=σεE = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}E=εσ​. The approximately uniform gap field gives V=EdV = EdV=Ed. Substitute:

V=QdϵA⇒C=QV=ϵAd=κϵ0Ad.V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon A}\Rightarrow C=\frac QV=\frac{\epsilon A}{d}=\frac{\kappa\epsilon_0 A}{d}.V=ϵAQd​⇒C=VQ​=dϵA​=dκϵ0​A​.

Here ε0≈8.85×10−12 Fm\varepsilon_{0} \approx 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{m}}ε0​≈8.85×10−12mF​ and κ\kappaκ is a dimensionless dielectric constant. Rearrangements are A=Cd(κε0)A = \frac{Cd}{\left( \kappa \varepsilon_{0} \right)}A=(κε0​)Cd​, d=κε0ACd = \frac{\kappa \varepsilon_{0} A}{C}d=Cκε0​A​, κ=Cd(ε0A)\kappa = \frac{Cd}{\left( \varepsilon_{0} A \right)}κ=(ε0​A)Cd​. The parallel-plate model needs plate dimensions much larger than gap d. Do not use the same equation for arbitrary conductor shapes.

Worked example — primary p. 14. C=1.0 FC = 1.0\,\mathrm{F}C=1.0F, d=1.0 mmd = 1.0\,\mathrm{mm}d=1.0mm in vacuum gives A=1×0.001(8.85×10−12)=1.13×108 m2A = \frac{1 \times 0.001}{\left( 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \right)} = 1.13 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}^{2}A=(8.85×10−12)1×0.001​=1.13×108m2. A missing milli prefix changes the answer by 1000.

Worked example — primary p. 14. A=2.0 m2A = 2.0\,\mathrm{m}^{2}A=2.0m2, d=5.0 mmd = 5.0\,\mathrm{mm}d=5.0mm, and V=10,000 VV = 10{,}000\,\mathrm{V}V=10,000V give C=3.54×10−9 F=0.00354 μFC = 3.54 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F} = 0.00354\,\mathrm{\mu F}C=3.54×10−9F=0.00354μF, Q=35.4 μCQ = 35.4\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q=35.4μC, and E=2.0×106 VmE = 2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}E=2.0×106mV​. Dielectrics: connected versus disconnected battery

A dielectric polarizes and increases capacitance when it fills the gap: Cnew=κColdC_{\mathrm{new}} = \kappa C_{\mathrm{old}}Cnew​=κCold​. It can mechanically separate plates and permit greater voltage before breakdown, depending on the material and conditions.

Quantity Battery stays connected Battery is disconnected, ideal isolated capacitor
Voltage Fixed by ideal battery Divides by κ\kappaκ
Free charge magnitude Multiplies by κ\kappaκ Fixed
Capacitance Multiplies by κ\kappaκ Multiplies by κ\kappaκ
Field in fully filled fixed gap Fixed Divides by κ\kappaκ
Stored energy Multiplies by κ\kappaκ Divides by κ\kappaκ

Derive these changes. Start with Q=CVQ = CVQ=CV. Fix V in the connected case or Q in the isolated case. Then use U=CV22U = \frac{CV^{2}}{2}U=2CV2​ or Q2(2 C)\frac{Q^{2}}{\left( 2\,\mathrm{C} \right)}(2C)Q2​. The connected capacitor can gain stored energy because the battery exchanges energy and charge. The isolated capacitor's energy decrease can become mechanical work during dielectric insertion.

Extensions — partial dielectric geometry. Two materials occupying side-by-side area fractions share the voltage, so C=ε0(κ1A1+κ2A2)dC = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} \left( \kappa_{1} A_{1} + \kappa_{2} A_{2} \right)}{d}C=dε0​(κ1​A1​+κ2​A2​)​. Layers stacked across the gap share the series charge, so 1C=d1(κ1ε0A)+d2(κ2ε0A)\frac{1}{C} = \frac{d_{1}}{\left( \kappa_{1} \varepsilon_{0} A \right)} + \frac{d_{2}}{\left( \kappa_{2} \varepsilon_{0} A \right)}C1​=(κ1​ε0​A)d1​​+(κ2​ε0​A)d2​​. Use the geometry to choose the connection model.

The voltage rises while charging. An additional dq requires work dU=V(q)dq=(qC)dqdU = V \left( q \right) dq = \left( \frac{q}{C} \right) dqdU=V(q)dq=(Cq​)dq. Integrate from zero to Q:

U=∫0QqC dq=Q22C=12QV=12CV2.U=\int_0^Q\frac qC\,dq=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12QV=\frac12CV^2.U=∫0Q​Cq​dq=2CQ2​=21​QV=21​CV2.

Multiplying the FINAL voltage by the entire charge gives QV, twice the stored energy. A linear voltage rise has average charging voltage V2\frac{V}{2}2V​. Rearranging gives V=(2UC)V = \sqrt{\left( \frac{2 U}{C} \right)}V=(C2U​)​, C=2UV2C = \frac{2 U}{V^{2}}C=V22U​, or Q=(2CU)Q = \sqrt{\left( 2 CU \right)}Q=(2CU)​, with magnitudes and physically positive C.

C=5.80 μFC = 5.80\,\mathrm{\mu F}C=5.80μF and V=400 VV = 400\,\mathrm{V}V=400V give U=0.5(5.80×10−6)(4002)=0.464 JU = 0.5 \left( 5.80 \times 10^{-6} \right) \left( 400^{2} \right) = 0.464\,\mathrm{J}U=0.5(5.80×10−6)(4002)=0.464J.
