Networks: derive series and parallel rules

Parallel branches share the SAME two nodes. Their voltages are equal and terminal charges add: Qtot=∑CiVQ_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum C_{i} VQtot​=∑Ci​V. Thus Ceq=∑CiC_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum C_{i}Ceq​=∑Ci​. Series capacitors in an initially uncharged isolated-intermediate-node chain carry equal charge magnitude. Their voltage drops add: Vtot=Q∑(1Ci)V_{\mathrm{tot}} = Q\sum \left( \frac{1}{C_{i}} \right)Vtot​=Q∑(Ci​1​), so 1Ceq=∑i1Ci\frac1{C_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\sum_i\frac1{C_i}Ceq​1​=∑i​Ci​1​.

For two series capacitors, Ceq=C1C2(C1+C2)C_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{C_{1} C_{2}}{\left( C_{1} + C_{2} \right)}Ceq​=(C1​+C2​)C1​C2​​. Solving for an unknown gives C2=CeqC1(C1−Ceq)C_{2} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{eq}}C_{1}}{\left( C_{1} - C_{\mathrm{eq}} \right)}C2​=(C1​−Ceq​)Ceq​C1​​, requiring C1>Ceq>0C_{1} > C_{\mathrm{eq}} > 0C1​>Ceq​>0. In parallel, C2=Ceq−C1>0C_{2} = C_{\mathrm{eq}} - C_{1} > 0C2​=Ceq​−C1​>0. Series equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest element; parallel equivalent capacitance exceeds each positive element.

Worked example — primary p. 24. Connect 6 μF6\,\mathrm{\mu F}6μF and 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF to 18 V18\,\mathrm{V}18V. Series: Ceq=2 μFC_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}Ceq​=2μF, Qeach=36 μCQ_{\mathrm{each}} = 36\,\mathrm{\mu C}Qeach​=36μC, V6=6 VV_{6} = 6\,\mathrm{V}V6​=6V, V3=12 VV_{3} = 12\,\mathrm{V}V3​=12V. Parallel: Ceq=9 μFC_{\mathrm{eq}} = 9\,\mathrm{\mu F}Ceq​=9μF, Veach=18 VV_{\mathrm{each}} = 18\,\mathrm{V}Veach​=18V, Q6=108 μCQ_{6} = 108\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q6​=108μC, Q3=54 μCQ_{3} = 54\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q3​=54μC. The smaller SERIES capacitor has the larger voltage because its charge magnitude is the same.

For a mixed network, label nodes before reducing it. Two nearby symbols are not necessarily parallel. Reduce a valid group, record its equivalent value, solve the terminal circuit, and then work backward. Use the original group’s shared Q or shared V to recover each element. Check ΣVi for series groups and ΣQi for parallel groups.

Worked extension — reduce, then restore the branches. Put 2 μF2\,\mathrm{\mu F}2μF and 4 μF4\,\mathrm{\mu F}4μF in parallel. Connect that group in series with 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF across 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V. The parallel group is 6 μF6\,\mathrm{\mu F}6μF. Its series equivalent with 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF is (6×3)(6+3)=2 μF\frac{\left( 6 \times 3 \right)}{\left( 6 + 3 \right)} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}(6+3)(6×3)​=2μF. The source transfers Q=2×12=24 μCQ = 2 \times 12 = 24\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q=2×12=24μC to each series unit.

The 6 μF6\,\mathrm{\mu F}6μF group has voltage 246=4 V\frac{24}{6} = 4\,\mathrm{V}624​=4V. The 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF capacitor has voltage 243=8 V\frac{24}{3} = 8\,\mathrm{V}324​=8V. Both parallel capacitors share 4 V4\,\mathrm{V}4V, so their charges are 8 μC8\,\mathrm{\mu C}8μC and 16 μC16\,\mathrm{\mu C}16μC. Their sum is the group's 24 μC24\,\mathrm{\mu C}24μC. Check energy: 12(2 μF)(122)=144 μJ\tfrac{1}{2} \left( 2\,\mathrm{\mu F} \right) \left( 12^{2} \right) = 144\,\mathrm{\mu J}21​(2μF)(122)=144μJ. The individual energies are 16, 32, and 96 μJ96\,\mathrm{\mu J}96μJ, which also sum to 144 μJ144\,\mathrm{\mu J}144μJ. A single equivalent capacitance alone does not reveal every branch voltage.

Charge-sharing extension. Disconnect two capacitors from their supplies and join their positive plates together. With no leakage, Vf=(C1V1+C2V2)(C1+C2)V_{f} = \frac{\left( C_{1} V_{1} + C_{2} V_{2} \right)}{\left( C_{1} + C_{2} \right)}Vf​=(C1​+C2​)(C1​V1​+C2​V2​)​. Reverse one capacitor's polarity by using a negative signed initial voltage. Final energy need not equal the sum of initial capacitor energies; the connection can dissipate energy. Charge conservation does not imply capacitor-energy conservation.

For C1=2 μFC_{1} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}C1​=2μF at 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V and C2=4 μFC_{2} = 4\,\mathrm{\mu F}C2​=4μF at 0 V0\,\mathrm{V}0V, Vf=4 VV_{f} = 4\,\mathrm{V}Vf​=4V. Initial stored energy is 144 μJ144\,\mathrm{\mu J}144μJ; final energy is 48 μJ48\,\mathrm{\mu J}48μJ. The difference, 96 μJ96\,\mathrm{\mu J}96μJ, leaves the capacitor fields during the transient. Real connections transfer it through resistance, radiation, or other losses. An ideal zero-resistance instantaneous connection is not a complete transient model.

From the plate fields to C=εAdC = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}C=dεA​

Sources: Primary pp. 7–13; companion pp. 1–4. Use large parallel plates, a uniform linear dielectric, and negligible edge effects.

  1. Write the free surface-charge density as σ=QA\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}σ=AQ​.
  2. Add the two ideal plate fields. The gap field is E=σεE = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}E=εσ​, not σ(2ε)\frac{\sigma}{\left( 2 \varepsilon \right)}(2ε)σ​.
  3. Use the uniform-gap potential difference magnitude V=EdV = EdV=Ed.
  4. Substitute σ=QA\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}σ=AQ​ to obtain V=Qd(εA)V = \frac{Qd}{\left( \varepsilon A \right)}V=(εA)Qd​.
  5. Divide charge by voltage: C=QV=εAdC = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}C=VQ​=dεA​.

Unit check. εAd\frac{\varepsilon A}{d}dεA​ has units (Fm)(m2)m=F\frac{\left( \frac{F}{m} \right) \left( m^{2} \right)}{m} = Fm(mF​)(m2)​=F. The dielectric constant κ=εε0\kappa = \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_{0}}κ=ε0​ε​ has no unit. Do not confuse κ\kappaκ with Coulomb's constant k.

The table gives κ=1\kappa = 1κ=1 for vacuum and about 1.00059 for air at 1 atm1\,\mathrm{atm}1atm. The usual classroom approximation uses air ≈ vacuum. Listed examples include Teflon 2.1, polyethylene 2.25, glass 5–10, and water 80.4. Capacitance depends on both geometry and the dielectric, not geometry alone when materials change.

Battery work and stored energy during dielectric insertion

This is a labeled extension. Initially C0C_{0}C0​ and V0V_{0}V0​ describe the capacitor. Insert a dielectric of constant κ\kappaκ quasistatically into the entire fixed gap, while an ideal battery stays connected.

  1. Find ΔQ=(κ−1)C0V0\Delta Q = \left( \kappa - 1 \right) C_{0} V_{0}ΔQ=(κ−1)C0​V0​ from Q=CVQ = CVQ=CV.

Wfield,mech=Wbattery−ΔU=12(κ−1)C0V02.W_{field,mech}=W_{battery}-\Delta U =\frac12(\kappa-1)C_0V_0^2.Wfield,mech​=Wbattery​−ΔU=21​(κ−1)C0​V02​.

For an isolated capacitor, the battery supplies no energy. Its field energy decreases from Q02(2C0)\frac{Q_{0}^{2}}{\left( 2 C_{0} \right)}(2C0​)Q02​​ to Q02(2κC0)\frac{Q_{0}^{2}}{\left( 2 \kappa C_{0} \right)}(2κC0​)Q02​​. The decrease can become mechanical work. State the electrical connection before applying energy conservation.

Applications — primary p. 26. A camera flash stores energy over a longer charging interval and releases it over a shorter interval. The same energy released in less time gives greater average power, Pavg=ΔUΔtP_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\Delta U}{\Delta t}Pavg​=ΔtΔU​. Capacitors also smooth changing supply voltages and provide brief charge pulses. Their circuit role depends on the connection, not merely the presence of a capacitor symbol.

Module 07 / Physics 2

Current and DC circuits: label nodes, currents, and polarity

Current, material properties, DC networks, Kirchhoff rules, and RC transients.

Topics in this module
Derive drift current and macroscopic resistanceTemperature, ohmic behavior, and resistor identificationElectrical power, energy, and internal resistanceDerive series and parallel resistor rulesKirchhoff rules: derive the equations and keep the signsRC charging and discharging: derive the exponentialsFinish the current, resistivity, and resistor-identification materialComplete the primary Ohm's-law and power exercisesRecover every series, parallel, and mixed-network resultKirchhoff examples: derive the signs and solve both supplied networksRC circuits: complete logarithms, limits, and switching checks

Current is signed charge flow per time: I=dQdtI = \frac{dQ}{dt}I=dtdQ​, or QΔt\frac{Q}{\Delta t}ΔtQ​ for a constant average flow. One ampere is one Cs\frac{C}{s}sC​. Conventional current points as positive charge would move. Electron drift in a metal points the opposite way. Random microscopic motion alone gives no net current. Current through a branch is a signed scalar; current density J is a vector.

Derive drift current and macroscopic resistance

In time Δt\Delta tΔt, carriers drift through volume AvdΔtAv_{d} \Delta tAvd​Δt. With number density n and charge magnitude |q|, charge crossing the area is nAvdΔt∣q∣nAv_{d} \Delta t \left| q \right|nAvd​Δt∣q∣. Divide by Δt\Delta tΔt:

I=n∣q∣Avd,J=I/A=n∣q∣vd,J=nqvd.I=n|q|Av_d,\quad J=I/A=n|q|v_d,\quad \mathbf J=nq\mathbf v_d.I=n∣q∣Avd​,J=I/A=n∣q∣vd​,J=nqvd​.

The vector expression keeps the signed charge. Carrier concentration has units m−3m^{-3}m−3, not Cm3\frac{C}{m^{3}}m3C​. Current from several carrier populations adds. J parallel to E is the simple isotropic ohmic model; it is not a universal statement for every medium and magnetic-field condition.

Worked examples — primary pp. 16–17. 29.3 C29.3\,\mathrm{C}29.3C in 7.84 s7.84\,\mathrm{s}7.84s gives 3.737 A3.737\,\mathrm{A}3.737A. A 0.010 A0.010\,\mathrm{A}0.010A calculator for 60 s60\,\mathrm{s}60s transfers 0.600 C0.600\,\mathrm{C}0.600C. J=50 Am2J = 50\,\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{m}^{2}}J=50m2A​, q=−0.10 Cq = - 0.10\,\mathrm{C}q=−0.10C, and vd=−2.0×10−4 msv_{d} = - 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}vd​=−2.0×10−4sm​ give n=J(qvd)=2.5×106 m−3n = \frac{J}{\left( qv_{d} \right)} = 2.5 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}n=(qvd​)J​=2.5×106m−3. The unusually large individual charge is the source's hypothetical value, not an electron charge.

For an ohmic isotropic material, E=ρJE = \rho JE=ρJ and conductivity σ=1ρ\sigma = \frac{1}{\rho}σ=ρ1​. Substitute E=VLE = \frac{V}{L}E=LV​ and J=IAJ = \frac{I}{A}J=AI​ for a uniform wire:

VL=ρIA⇒V=IR,R=ρLA,ρ=RAL.\frac VL=\rho\frac IA\Rightarrow V=IR,\quad R=\frac{\rho L}{A},\quad \rho=\frac{RA}{L}.LV​=ρAI​⇒V=IR,R=AρL​,ρ=LRA​.

Resistivity ρ\rhoρ has units Ω·m; resistance R has units Ω. For a circular wire A=πr2=πd24A = \pi r^{2} = \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}A=πr2=4πd2​. Doubling LENGTH at fixed area doubles R. Doubling DIAMETER at fixed length divides R by four. For the same wire stretched without volume change, A=VwireLA = \frac{V_{\mathrm{wire}}}{L}A=LVwire​​, so R=ρL2VwireR = \frac{\rho L^{2}}{V_{\mathrm{wire}}}R=Vwire​ρL2​ if resistivity stays constant.

Temperature, ohmic behavior, and resistor identification

Near a reference temperature, R=R0[1+α(T−T0)]R = R_{0} \left[ 1 + \alpha \left( T - T_{0} \right) \right]R=R0​[1+α(T−T0​)], and similarly for resistivity. Rearrange α=(RR0−1)(T−T0)\alpha = \frac{\left( \frac{R}{R_{0}} - 1 \right)}{\left( T - T_{0} \right)}α=(T−T0​)(R0​R​−1)​. This linear approximation can fail over a large temperature range. Do not confuse the resistance-temperature coefficient with thermal-expansion α\alphaα. R0R_{0}R0​ is resistance when used in the R equation, despite the source's occasional “resistivity” label.

Ohm's law means a linear V–I relation under stable material conditions. A lamp heating up need not have a constant resistance. Carbon/semiconductor temperature behavior can differ from metals.

The source includes resistor color bands. For a four-band resistor, the first two colors give digits, the third gives a power-of-ten multiplier, and the fourth gives tolerance. Digit sequence: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Gold/silver commonly represent multipliers 10−110−2\frac{10^{-1}}{10^{-2}}10−210−1​ or tolerances ±5%/±10%. Read the band roles and orientation, not only the colors.

Electrical power, energy, and internal resistance

An amount dq crossing voltage V transfers energy dW=VdqdW = VdqdW=Vdq. Divide by dt:

P=VI,PR=I2R=VR2/R,Eenergy=Pt.P=VI,\quad P_R=I^2R=V_R^2/R,\quad E_{energy}=Pt.P=VI,PR​=I2R=VR2​/R,Eenergy​=Pt.

The resistor substitutions require Ohm's law. A kilowatt-hour is an ENERGY unit: 1 kWh=3.6×106 J1\,\mathrm{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{J}1kWh=3.6×106J. It is not “kilowatts per hour.” At fixed V, increasing R lowers resistor power; at fixed I, increasing R raises it.

A real source has emf E\mathcal{E}E and internal resistance r. For discharging current I, terminal voltage V=E−IrV = \mathcal{E} - IrV=E−Ir and I=E(R+r)I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{\left( R + r \right)}I=(R+r)E​. During charging with current driven into the positive terminal, V=E+IrV = \mathcal{E} + IrV=E+Ir under that stated convention. Emf is energy supplied per charge, not a mechanical force.

Worked example — companion heating element. R=20ΩR = 20 \OmegaR=20Ω on 120 V120\,\mathrm{V}120V gives I=6 AI = 6\,\mathrm{A}I=6A and P=720 WP = 720\,\mathrm{W}P=720W. In 15 min=900 s15\,\mathrm{min} = 900\,\mathrm{s}15min=900s, energy: 648,000 J=0.18 kWh648{,}000\,\mathrm{J} = 0.18\,\mathrm{kWh}648,000J=0.18kWh. Increasing R to 30 Ω30\,\Omega30Ω at the same voltage gives 480 W480\,\mathrm{W}480W, not greater power.

Derive series and parallel resistor rules

Series resistors have a common current if there is no branch at their connecting node. Vtot=∑IRiV_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum IR_{i}Vtot​=∑IRi​ gives Req=∑RiR_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum R_{i}Req​=∑Ri​. Therefore ViVtot=RiReq\frac{V_{i}}{V_{\mathrm{tot}}} = \frac{R_{i}}{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}Vtot​Vi​​=Req​Ri​​: the voltage-divider relation.

Parallel resistors share the same two nodes and voltage. Itot=∑iVRiI_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_i\frac{V}{R_i}Itot​=∑i​Ri​V​ gives 1Req=∑i1Ri\frac1{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\sum_i\frac1{R_i}Req​1​=∑i​Ri​1​. For two, Req=R1R2(R1+R2)R_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{R_{1} R_{2}}{\left( R_{1} + R_{2} \right)}Req​=(R1​+R2​)R1​R2​​. Their current ratio is I1I2=R2R1\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}} = \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}}I2​I1​​=R1​R2​​. An equivalent parallel resistance must be smaller than the smallest positive branch resistance.

Worked example. Put 3 Ω3\,\Omega3Ω and 6 Ω6\,\Omega6Ω in parallel across 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V. Req=2ΩR_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2 \OmegaReq​=2Ω; branch currents are 4 A4\,\mathrm{A}4A and 2 A2\,\mathrm{A}2A; total is 6 A6\,\mathrm{A}6A. Total power: 12×6=72 W12 \times 6 = 72\,\mathrm{W}12×6=72W, also 42×3+22×6=72 W4^{2} \times 3 + 2^{2} \times 6 = 72\,\mathrm{W}42×3+22×6=72W. A series 4 Ω4\,\Omega4Ω added before that group gives 6 Ω6\,\Omega6Ω overall. The source current becomes 2 A2\,\mathrm{A}2A, the parallel-group drop becomes 4 V4\,\mathrm{V}4V, and its branch currents become 43A\frac{4}{3} A34​A and 23A\frac{2}{3} A32​A.

An ideal ammeter goes in SERIES and has zero resistance. An ideal voltmeter goes in PARALLEL and has infinite resistance. An ideal wire shorts points into one node. A shorted resistor has zero voltage, not its previous unmodified branch voltage. Do not reduce an arbitrary bridge as series/parallel when the required node conditions fail.

Kirchhoff rules: derive the equations and keep the signs

KCL follows conservation of charge at a steady node: ∑Iin=∑Iout\sum I_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum I_{\mathrm{out}}∑Iin​=∑Iout​. KVL follows energy balance around a lumped DC loop: ∑ΔV=0\sum \Delta V = 0∑ΔV=0. A resistor traversed with the chosen current gives −IR; traversed against it gives +IR. Across an ideal battery, negative-to-positive gives +E+ \mathcal{E}+E and the reverse gives −E- \mathcal{E}−E.

Choose arbitrary current directions, write independent equations, and solve them simultaneously. A negative answer reverses the assumed direction; it is not a negative physical resistance. Do not change an assumed arrow midway through the algebra.

Source problems · full working

Finish the current, resistivity, and resistor-identification material

Current carriers. The primary's “flow of electrons” definition describes a metal, but current more generally means net charge flow. Positive and negative ions can also carry current. A closed circuit provides a continuous conducting path. An open branch carries no steady conduction current in this model. A short circuit provides a low-resistance path; an actual source's internal resistance still limits its current.

Circuit symbols — primary p. 37. The longer battery line marks the positive terminal. An A in a circle denotes an ammeter in the measured branch. A V in a circle denotes a voltmeter connected across two nodes. A connection dot identifies joined wires. Label the nodes before deciding whether two components share a voltage.

Current and the body — primary p. 15. The source table associates increasing current with sensation, muscle effects, disrupted breathing, and heart effects. Its ranges are illustrative, not universal thresholds. Effects also depend on the current path and contact duration. OSHA's electrical-safety material explains these dependencies. The original table remains available in the source reader.

Drift, collision time, and microscopic Ohm's law

Source starting point: Primary p. 7. The additional algebra uses a simple relaxation-time model.

  1. Between collisions, the carrier acceleration is a=qEma = \frac{qE}{m}a=mqE​.
  2. The model's mean drift velocity is vd=qEτcollisionmv_{d} = \frac{qE\tau _{\mathrm{collision}}}{m}vd​=mqEτcollision​​.
  3. Insert vd into J=nqvdJ = nqv_{d}J=nqvd​.
  4. Compare the result with J=σEJ = \sigma EJ=σE.
J=nq2τcollisionmE,σ=nq2τcollisionm,ρ=mnq2τcollision.\begin{gathered}\mathbf J=\frac{nq^2\tau_{collision}}m\mathbf E, \\\sigma=\frac{nq^2\tau_{collision}}m, \\\rho=\frac{m}{nq^2\tau_{collision}}.\end{gathered}J=mnq2τcollision​​E,σ=mnq2τcollision​​,ρ=nq2τcollision​m​.​

The squared charge makes σ\sigmaσ positive for either carrier sign. For electrons, vd opposes E while J points along E. This is a microscopic model for suitable materials; it is not an exact conductivity theory for every substance.

The companion also lists conductors, semiconductors, and insulators. Metals generally have low resistivity. Insulators have much higher resistivity. Semiconductor resistivity strongly depends on temperature and impurities. Four, five, and six bands. Four bands use two significant digits, a multiplier, and tolerance. Five bands use three significant digits, a multiplier, and tolerance. Six bands add a temperature coefficient, commonly expressed in parts per million per kelvin. The source's pictured six-band resistor is green–blue–black–red–gold–yellow.

Kirchhoff examples: derive the signs and solve both supplied networks

Source correction — primary p. 66. Different independent loops do not have to use the same traversal direction. Each loop can use either direction. Keep the signs consistent within that traversal. Reversing one complete loop equation multiplies it by −1 without changing the physical solution.

Independent equations. Repeating the junction equation at both ends of the same branches does not create new information. The outer loop is a combination of the two inner loops in the source example. Use enough independent equations for the unknown branch currents.

ln⁡qQ0=−tRC⇒q=Q0e−t/RC,VC=V0e−t/RC,t=RCln⁡V0VC.\ln\frac{q}{Q_0}=-\frac{t}{RC} \Rightarrow q=Q_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad V_C=V_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad t=RC\ln\frac{V_0}{V_C}.lnQ0​q​=−RCt​⇒q=Q0​e−t/RC,VC​=V0​e−t/RC,t=RClnVC​V0​​.

The logarithm uses a dimensionless ratio. For a decay fraction f=VCV0f = \frac{V_{C}}{V_{0}}f=V0​VC​​, use 0<f≤10 < f \le 10<f≤1. Reaching exactly zero takes infinite time in the ideal exponential model.

Initial and final conditions. An initially uncharged capacitor has VC(0)=0V_{C} \left( 0 \right) = 0VC​(0)=0 and initially behaves as a zero-voltage element in the charging circuit. At DC steady state, its current tends to zero. A precharged capacitor is not initially a zero-voltage element. Use VC(t)=Vf+(Vinitial−Vf)exp⁡(−tτ)V_{C} \left( t \right) = V_{f} + \left( V_{\mathrm{initial}} - V_{f} \right) \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\tau} \right)VC​(t)=Vf​+(Vinitial​−Vf​)exp(−τt​) when the initial voltage is nonzero.

Timing applications. Wipers, traffic-light timers, camera flashes, and pacemaker timing circuits use charging or discharging intervals. The elementary RC model explains a time scale; it does not represent every control function inside those devices.

Module 08 / Physics 2

Magnetic fields: the cross product fixes the direction

Magnetic forces, current-loop torque, wire fields, and Ampere law.

Topics in this module
Force on a moving charge and on a wireCircular and helical motion: derived extensionsTorque on a current loopLong wires, parallel-current force, and Ampere's lawSolenoids, cores, and scope of symmetryMagnetism, field notation, and the three right-hand rulesSolve both source magnetic-force examples in fullTorque: derive the area factor and use the actual angleSource-wire fields, parallel-wire force, and solenoids

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Breaking a bar magnet makes smaller dipoles, not isolated ordinary north and south poles. Outside a bar magnet, conventional field lines go north to south; they continue through the magnet to form closed loops. A compass's north-seeking end gives the local field direction. Earth's geographic and magnetic pole descriptions are not identical.

Oersted's current-carrying wire deflects a compass, showing that current creates a magnetic field. Do not confuse this source-field right-hand grip rule with the force cross-product rule.

Force on a moving charge and on a wire

FB=qv×B,FB=∣q∣vBsin⁡θ.\mathbf F_B=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B,\quad F_B=|q|vB\sin\theta.FB​=qv×B,FB​=∣q∣vBsinθ.

θ\thetaθ is between velocity and B. For positive q, curl the right-hand direction from v toward B; reverse the result for negative q. A charge at rest has no magnetic force from this law. Parallel or antiparallel motion gives zero magnetic force, not maximum force. Perpendicular motion gives the maximum magnitude.

Derive wire force. A segment of length L and cross-sectional area A contains nAL carriers. Each has transverse force qvd×Bqv_{d} \times Bqvd​×B. Sum and use I=n∣q∣AvdI = n \left| q \right| Av_{d}I=n∣q∣Avd​ to obtain F=IL×BF = IL \times BF=IL×B, with L directed along conventional current. For a curved wire use I∫dl×BI \int dl \times BI∫dl×B. Only the length inside the field contributes.

Worked example — primary p. 14. I=5.0 AI = 5.0\,\mathrm{A}I=5.0A east; L=1.0 mL = 1.0\,\mathrm{m}L=1.0m; B=1.20 TB = 1.20\,\mathrm{T}B=1.20T at 45° north of east. F=5×1×1.2sin⁡45∘=4.243 NF = 5 \times 1 \times 1.2 \sin 45^{\circ} = 4.243\,\mathrm{N}F=5×1×1.2sin45∘=4.243N. East × north points up in an east/north/up coordinate system.

Worked example — primary p. 20. An electron moves +x at 8.0×106 ms8.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}8.0×106sm​. A 0.025 T0.025\,\mathrm{T}0.025T field makes 60° to +x in the +y half of the xy plane. Magnitude: evBsin⁡60∘=2.775×10−14 Ne v B \sin 60^{\circ} = 2.775 \times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{N}evBsin60∘=2.775×10−14N. Since +x×+y=+z+ x \times + y = + z+x×+y=+z, the electron's force is −z. Without specifying the y-half-plane, the angle alone does not fix that sign.

Circular and helical motion: derived extensions

A magnetic force does no work on a point charge because v⋅(v×B)=0v \cdot \left( v \times B \right) = 0v⋅(v×B)=0. It changes direction, not speed, in a purely magnetic uniform field. For perpendicular motion, set ∣q∣vB=mv2r\left| q \right| vB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}∣q∣vB=rmv2​:

r=mv⊥∣q∣B,ωc=∣q∣Bm,T=2πm∣q∣B.r=\frac{mv_\perp}{|q|B},\quad \omega_c=\frac{|q|B}{m},\quad T=\frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}.r=∣q∣Bmv⊥​​,ωc​=m∣q∣B​,T=∣q∣B2πm​.

For an oblique entry, v∥v_{\parallel}v∥​ remains constant, while v⊥v_{\perp}v⊥​ circles. Helical pitch: p=v∥Tp=v_{\parallel}Tp=v∥​T. These are nonrelativistic formulas. Combining kinetic energy K with r gives r=(2mK)(∣q∣B)r = \frac{\sqrt{\left( 2 mK \right)}}{\left( \left| q \right| B \right)}r=(∣q∣B)(2mK)​​ for perpendicular entry. In crossed perpendicular E and B fields, straight undeflected motion requires ∣q∣E=∣q∣vB\left| q \right| E = \left| q \right| vB∣q∣E=∣q∣vB, so v=EBv = \frac{E}{B}v=BE​ with force directions opposing.

Torque on a current loop

Opposite sides of a loop in uniform B have equal and opposite forces. Net force can vanish while torque remains. The lever-arm geometry yields:

μ=NIA,τ=μ×B,τ=NIABsin⁡θ,U=−μ⋅B.\begin{gathered}\boldsymbol\mu=NI\mathbf A,\\\boldsymbol\tau=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B,\\\tau=NIAB\sin\theta,\\U=-\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B.\end{gathered}μ=NIA,τ=μ×B,τ=NIABsinθ,U=−μ⋅B.​

Here θ\thetaθ is between the AREA NORMAL and B, not between the loop's plane and B. For angle ϕ\phiϕ to the plane, sin⁡θ=cos⁡ϕ\sin \theta = \cos \phisinθ=cosϕ. Maximum torque occurs when the normal is perpendicular to B. Zero torque occurs when the normal is parallel or antiparallel; the parallel orientation has the lower potential energy.

Worked example — primary p. 28. Diameter: 20.0 cm20.0\,\mathrm{cm}20.0cm, so r=0.100 mr = 0.100\,\mathrm{m}r=0.100m and A=π(0.100)2A = \pi \left( 0.100 \right)^{2}A=π(0.100)2. With N=10N = 10N=10, I=3.00 AI = 3.00\,\mathrm{A}I=3.00A, B=2.00 TB = 2.00\,\mathrm{T}B=2.00T, τmax=1.885 N⋅m\tau _{\mathrm{max}} = 1.885\,\mathrm{N} \cdot mτmax​=1.885N⋅m and τmin=0\tau _{\mathrm{min}} = 0τmin​=0. The primary's side-force label involving IAB should not be read as the wire-force law: force uses a LENGTH, while torque uses an AREA.

A galvanometer turns a current-carrying coil against a restoring effect. Analog meters build on that principle. A motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy; a loudspeaker moves a coil and cone with a varying force.

Long wires, parallel-current force, and Ampere's law

Magnetostatic Ampere's law is ∮B⋅dl=μ0Ienclosed\oint B \cdot dl = \mu_{0} I_{\mathrm{enclosed}}∮B⋅dl=μ0​Ienclosed​. For a long straight wire, cylindrical symmetry makes B constant on a circular path. Therefore B(2πr)=μ0IB \left( 2 \pi r \right) = \mu_{0} IB(2πr)=μ0​I:

B=μ0I2πr,FL=I2B1=μ0I1I22πd.B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r},\quad \frac FL=I_2B_1=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi d}.B=2πrμ0​I​,LF​=I2​B1​=2πdμ0​I1​I2​​.

Use μ0≈4π×10−7 T⋅mA\mu_{0} \approx \frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{T} \cdot m}{A}μ0​≈A4π×10−7T⋅m​ for course calculations. Same-direction parallel currents attract; opposite directions repel. The distance is between the wire axes, not wire length. Fields from several wires add as vectors.

Worked examples — primary pp. 33 and 36. A 25 A25\,\mathrm{A}25A upward wire at r=0.10 mr = 0.10\,\mathrm{m}r=0.10m gives B=5.0×10−5 TB = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}B=5.0×10−5T. At a point north of that wire, the direction is west. Two wires carrying 8.0 A8.0\,\mathrm{A}8.0A, separated by 0.0030 m0.0030\,\mathrm{m}0.0030m over 2.0 m2.0\,\mathrm{m}2.0m length, exert F=8.533×10−3 NF = 8.533 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}F=8.533×10−3N. Their relative current directions determine attraction or repulsion.

Solenoids, cores, and scope of symmetry

For an ideal long solenoid, an Amperian rectangle has negligible external contribution. Enclosed current is (Nℓ)I\left( \frac{N}{\ell} \right) I(ℓN​)I times its interior path length. Thus B=μ0(Nℓ)IB = \mu_{0} \left( \frac{N}{\ell} \right) IB=μ0​(ℓN​)I, or μnI\mu nIμnI in an ideal linear core. ℓ is the SOLENOID length, not the total winding-wire length.

Worked example — primary p. 39. N=420N = 420N=420, ℓ=0.12 m\ell = 0.12\,\mathrm{m}ℓ=0.12m, I=2.0 AI = 2.0\,\mathrm{A}I=2.0A. B=4π×10−7(4200.12)(2)=8.796×10−3 T\begin{aligned}B &= 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \left( \frac{420}{0.12} \right) \left( 2 \right) \\&= 8.796 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}\end{aligned}B​=4π×10−7(0.12420​)(2)=8.796×10−3T​ near the center in the long-solenoid approximation.

An iron core can increase field strongly, but a constant relative permeability is only an approximation; real cores can saturate and show hysteresis. Ampere's law alone does not let you pull B outside the integral without sufficient symmetry. For a circular coil's center, a separate Biot–Savart integration gives B=μ0NI(2R)B = \frac{\mu_{0} NI}{\left( 2 R \right)}B=(2R)μ0​NI​; do not substitute the long-solenoid formula into a single-loop problem.

Derive the circular-coil result. Biot–Savart gives dB=μ0Idlsin⁡θ(4πr2)dB = \frac{\mu_{0} I dl \sin \theta}{\left( 4 \pi r^{2} \right)}dB=(4πr2)μ0​Idlsinθ​. At a loop's center, r=Rr = Rr=R and every tangent element is perpendicular to its radius. All field contributions point along the same axis. Integrate dl around circumference 2πR and multiply by N:

Bcenter=μ0NI4πR2∮dl=μ0NI4πR2(2πR)=μ0NI2R.B_{center}=\frac{\mu_0NI}{4\pi R^2}\oint dl=\frac{\mu_0NI}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R)=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2R}.Bcenter​=4πR2μ0​NI​∮dl=4πR2μ0​NI​(2πR)=2Rμ0​NI​.

For 20 turns, 0.050 m0.050\,\mathrm{m}0.050m radius, and 2.0 A2.0\,\mathrm{A}2.0A, B≈5.027×10−4 TB \approx 5.027 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}B≈5.027×10−4T. This formula describes thin coincident loops. A long coil uses the solenoid approximation instead. A magnetic field created by this coil can exert force on another wire; do not substitute the wire's own field into a simple external-field force calculation.

Worked trajectory extension. A proton enters perpendicular to 0.20 T0.20\,\mathrm{T}0.20T at 1.0×106 ms1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}1.0×106sm​. Use mp=1.67×10−27 kgm_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}mp​=1.67×10−27kg and e=1.602×10−19 Ce = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}e=1.602×10−19C. Its radius is 0.05212 m0.05212\,\mathrm{m}0.05212m and period is 3.275×10−7 s3.275 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s}3.275×10−7s. Doubling the speed doubles the radius but leaves the nonrelativistic period unchanged. A parallel velocity component adds a helical displacement instead of changing this perpendicular radius.

Source problems · full working

Magnetism, field notation, and the three right-hand rules

Source context — primary pp. 4–11. The historical material describes magnetite and the name Magnesia. A magnetized needle aligns with the local field. Either end of a magnet can attract an initially unmagnetized iron nail because the nail becomes magnetized. Splitting a magnet produces smaller dipoles. It does not separate an ordinary bar magnet into isolated north and south poles.

Earth and a compass. The geographic poles describe the rotation axis. Magnetic-pole locations and the local field direction differ from that axis. Near geographic north, Earth's field can attract a compass's north-seeking end. Keep the pole-naming convention separate from the field direction used in a force calculation.

Question Right-hand operation What the result means
Field around a straight wire Point the thumb along conventional current; curl the fingers Finger curl gives B around the wire
Force on a current-carrying segment Form L×BL \times BL×B, with L along conventional current The cross product gives the force direction
Force on a moving positive charge Form v×Bv \times Bv×B The result gives force for positive q
Force on a negative charge Find v×Bv \times Bv×B, then reverse it Reversal accounts for negative q

Use a dot ⊙ for a vector out of the page and a cross ⊗ for a vector into the page. In a right-handed coordinate system, x×y=zx \times y = zx×y=z, y×z=xy \times z = xy×z=x, and z×x=yz \times x = yz×x=y. Reversing either factor reverses the cross product.

Units. 1 T=1 NAm=1 N⋅s(C⋅m)=1 Wbm2\begin{aligned}1\,\mathrm{T} &= 1\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{A} \mathrm{m}} \\&= \frac{1\,\mathrm{N} \cdot s}{\left( C \cdot m \right)} \\&= \frac{1\,\mathrm{Wb}}{m^{2}}\end{aligned}1T​=1AmN​=(C⋅m)1N⋅s​=m21Wb​​ Also, 1 T=1041\,\mathrm{T} = 10^{4}1T=104 gauss. Convert 3.0 mm3.0\,\mathrm{mm}3.0mm to 0.0030 m0.0030\,\mathrm{m}0.0030m before using a wire-spacing formula.

Derivation∴

Wire-force law from the motion of charge carriers

Source laws: Primary pp. 12–17. Let the carrier number density be n, wire cross section A, and segment length L. Use a uniform external field.

  1. Count the carriers inside the segment: Ncarriers=nALN_{\mathrm{carriers}} = nALNcarriers​=nAL.
  2. Add their magnetic forces: Ftotal=nALq(vd×B)F_{\mathrm{total}} = nALq \left( v_{d} \times B \right)Ftotal​=nALq(vd​×B).
  3. Use the signed carrier-current relation nqvd=Jnqv_{d} = Jnqvd​=J, with conventional-current direction encoded in J.
  4. Replace JA by the current and direct the length vector along that current.
F=IL×B,F=ILBsin⁡θ.\mathbf F=I\mathbf L\times\mathbf B, \qquad F=ILB\sin\theta.F=IL×B,F=ILBsinθ.

This derivation removes the microscopic carrier density and drift speed. L means the length inside the field. For a curved path in a nonuniform field, integrate Idl×BI dl \times BIdl×B instead of using one segment's product.

Recover an unknown field or angle from a force measurement

Start with F=∣q∣vBsin⁡θF = \left| q \right| vB\sin \thetaF=∣q∣vBsinθ or F=ILBsin⁡θF = ILB\sin \thetaF=ILBsinθ. If the geometry is perpendicular, sin⁡θ=1\sin \theta = 1sinθ=1.

B=F∣q∣vsin⁡θ,v=F∣q∣Bsin⁡θ,sin⁡θ=F∣q∣vB.B=\frac{F}{|q|v\sin\theta},\qquad v=\frac{F}{|q|B\sin\theta},\qquad \sin\theta=\frac{F}{|q|vB}.B=∣q∣vsinθF​,v=∣q∣BsinθF​,sinθ=∣q∣vBF​.

For a wire, replace |q|v by IL. A sine value larger than one signals inconsistent data or a wrong equation. In 0°–180°, both θ\thetaθ and 180∘−θ180^{\circ} - \theta180∘−θ have the same sine. Magnitude data alone cannot distinguish those directions. Parallel motion gives zero force even in a nonzero field.

Torque: derive the area factor and use the actual angle

Derivation∴

Why a current loop has torque NIABsin⁡θNIAB\sin \thetaNIABsinθ

Sources: Primary pp. 25–28. Let a rectangular loop have side length a along one pair of opposite forces and separation b between them.

  1. Each active side feels force F=IaBF = IaBF=IaB for the perpendicular-field component in the stated geometry.
  2. The perpendicular lever arm between the forces is bsin⁡θb\sin \thetabsinθ, where θ\thetaθ measures the area normal relative to B.
  3. Add the two moments as a force couple: τ=F(bsin⁡θ)\tau = F \left( b\sin \theta \right)τ=F(bsinθ).
  4. Substitute A=abA = abA=ab and multiply by N turns.
τ=NIabBsin⁡θ=NIABsin⁡θ.\tau=NIabB\sin\theta=NIAB\sin\theta.τ=NIabBsinθ=NIABsinθ.

Equal and opposite side forces can cancel the net force while their torques add. Primary p. 27's side-force expression “IAB” uses area where a length is needed. Force uses ILB; torque uses NIAB.

Circular coil: maximum, minimum, and an intermediate angle

Source problem: Primary p. 28. Given: Diameter 0.200 m0.200\,\mathrm{m}0.200m, N=10N = 10N=10, I=3.00 AI = 3.00\,\mathrm{A}I=3.00A, B=2.00 TB = 2.00\,\mathrm{T}B=2.00T.

  1. Halve the diameter: r=0.100 mr = 0.100\,\mathrm{m}r=0.100m.
  2. Find the one-turn area: A=πr2=0.0314159 m2A = \pi r^{2} = 0.0314159\,\mathrm{m}^{2}A=πr2=0.0314159m2.
  3. Find τmax=NIAB=1.88496 N⋅m\tau _{\mathrm{max}} = NIAB = 1.88496\,\mathrm{N} \cdot mτmax​=NIAB=1.88496N⋅m.
  4. Set the area normal perpendicular to B for the maximum. Set it parallel or antiparallel for τmin=0\tau _{\mathrm{min}} = 0τmin​=0.
  5. For a labeled extension at θ=30∘\theta = 30^{\circ}θ=30∘ to the normal, τ=τmaxsin⁡30∘=0.942478 N⋅m\tau = \tau _{\mathrm{max}}\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.942478\,\mathrm{N} \cdot mτ=τmax​sin30∘=0.942478N⋅m.

Angle check. If 30° is measured to the plane instead, θnormal=60∘\theta _{\mathrm{normal}} = 60^{\circ}θnormal​=60∘, giving τ≈1.63242 N⋅m\tau \approx 1.63242\,\mathrm{N} \cdot mτ≈1.63242N⋅m. The reference line changes the answer.

Derivation∴

Magnetic-loop potential energy from the torque

This is a labeled extension of the source's torque model. Keep the current, loop area, and applied field constant, so μ=NIA\mu = NIAμ=NIA stays constant. The magnetic torque turns a loop toward alignment with B. Its signed angular component is τmag=−μBsin⁡θ\tau _{\mathrm{mag}} = - \mu B\sin \thetaτmag​=−μBsinθ when positive θ\thetaθ increases the normal-to-field angle.

For a quasistatic increase dθd\thetadθ, an external agent supplies τexternal=+μBsin⁡θ\tau _{\mathrm{external}} = + \mu B\sin \thetaτexternal​=+μBsinθ. Thus dU=τexternaldθdU = \tau _{\mathrm{external}}d\thetadU=τexternal​dθ. Integrating and choosing zero energy at θ=90∘\theta = 90^{\circ}θ=90∘ gives U=−μBcos⁡θU = - \mu B\cos \thetaU=−μBcosθ. Alignment at θ=0\theta = 0θ=0 has minimum energy −μB- \mu B−μB. Anti-alignment at θ=π\theta = \piθ=π has maximum energy +μB+ \mu B+μB. Both have zero torque, but only the first is a stable orientation in this simple model.

Devices — primary pp. 29–31. A galvanometer balances magnetic torque against a restoring torque. In a linear spring model, κtorsionϕ=NIAB\kappa _{\mathrm{torsion}}\phi = NIABκtorsion​ϕ=NIAB for a radial-field meter, so its deflection can indicate current. A motor uses continuing electromagnetic torque to produce rotation. A loudspeaker uses a coil's magnetic force to move its attached cone. An ohmmeter also needs an internal source and associated circuitry; the galvanometer alone does not directly measure resistance.

Field north of an upward 25 A25\,\mathrm{A}25A wire

Parallel-wire force and its attraction or repulsion

Sources: Primary pp. 34–36. Wire 1 creates B1=μ0I1(2πd)B_{1} = \frac{\mu_{0} I_{1}}{\left( 2 \pi d \right)}B1​=(2πd)μ0​I1​​ at wire 2. For parallel wires, this field is perpendicular to wire 2. Apply F2=I2LB1F_{2} = I_{2} LB_{1}F2​=I2​LB1​:

F2=μ0I1I2L2πd,FL=μ0I1I22πd.F_2=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2L}{2\pi d},\qquad \frac FL=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi d}.F2​=2πdμ0​I1​I2​L​,LF​=2πdμ0​I1​I2​​.

Use the grip rule for B1B_{1}B1​, then L2×B1L_{2} \times B_{1}L2​×B1​ for the second force. Matching current directions give forces toward each other. Opposite current directions give forces away from each other. Repeating the calculation on wire 1 gives the same force magnitude.

Calculate FL=(4π×10−7)(8)(8)(2π×0.0030)=0.00426667 Nm\begin{aligned}\frac{F}{L} &= \frac{\left( 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \right) \left( 8 \right) \left( 8 \right)}{\left( 2 \pi \times 0.0030 \right)} \\&= 0.00426667\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m}}\end{aligned}LF​​=(2π×0.0030)(4π×10−7)(8)(8)​=0.00426667mN​​

Derivation∴

Ampere's law inside a long solenoid

Sources: Primary pp. 37–42. Use a rectangular Amperian path with an interior segment of length x parallel to the solenoid axis.

  1. The transverse path segments have B perpendicular to dl, so their dot-product contributions vanish.
  2. Neglect the outside field in the ideal long-solenoid approximation.
  3. The interior segment contributes Bx.
  4. If n=Nℓn = \frac{N}{\ell}n=ℓN​ is turns per unit solenoid length, the path encloses nx turns. Its enclosed current is nxI.
  5. Apply Ampere's law and cancel x.
Bx=μ0(nxI)⇒B=μ0nI=μ0NℓI.Bx=\mu_0(nxI)\Rightarrow B=\mu_0nI =\mu_0\frac{N}{\ell}I.Bx=μ0​(nxI)⇒B=μ0​nI=μ0​ℓN​I.

The Amperian-path length x cancels. The physical solenoid length ℓ remains. It is not the total length of wire used in the winding.

The source's 420-turn solenoid

Source: Primary p. 39. Given: N=420N = 420N=420, ℓ=12 cm=0.12 m\ell = 12\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.12\,\mathrm{m}ℓ=12cm=0.12m, and I=2.0 AI = 2.0\,\mathrm{A}I=2.0A.

  2. Calculate B=(4π×10−7)(3500)(2.0)=0.00879646 T\begin{aligned}B &= \left( 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \right) \left( 3500 \right) \left( 2.0 \right) \\&= 0.00879646\,\mathrm{T}\end{aligned}B​=(4π×10−7)(3500)(2.0)=0.00879646T​

Module 09 / Physics 2

Induction: change in flux, not merely the presence of a magnet

Changing flux, Lenz law, induced fields, transformers, and RL circuits.

Topics in this module
Magnetic flux and all three routes to a changing fluxFaraday's law and the full product derivativeLenz's law with four direction casesMotional emf from two derivationsGenerators, microphones, transformers, and eddy currentsMutual/self-inductance and stored magnetic energyRL growth, decay, and arbitrary initial currentFlux signs, partial overlap, and the induction experimentFull Faraday and transformer solutionsSolve Lenz's law and motional-emf cases step by stepThe missing distinction: induced electric fields are not electrostatic fieldsMutual inductance, self-inductance, and complete RL decay

An induced emf can exist without a closed conducting circuit. A closed path is required for the ordinary induced current examples. A stationary loop in a time-varying magnetic field can have emf even when no wire moves. Conversely, motion that leaves the relevant flux unchanged need not produce a net loop emf.

Magnetic flux and all three routes to a changing flux

ΦB=∫B⋅dA,ΦB=BAcos⁡θ for uniform B.\Phi_B=\int\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A,\quad \Phi_B=BA\cos\theta\ \text{for uniform }B.ΦB​=∫B⋅dA,ΦB​=BAcosθ for uniform B.

The angle is between B and the AREA NORMAL. If a problem gives the angle to the plane, use the complementary angle. One weber is one T⋅m2T \cdot m^{2}T⋅m2. A field perpendicular to the plane produces maximum flux magnitude; a field parallel to the plane produces zero flux.

If B occupies only an overlap area, integrate over that region. Primary p. 10 has flux BA2BA_{2}BA2​, not BA1BA_{1}BA1​, when the field is confined to the smaller perpendicular overlap area A2A_{2}A2​. Treat “zero outside the field region” explicitly.

Faraday's law and the full product derivative

Faraday's law is a fundamental induction law in this course. For N turns linking the same flux, E=−NdΦBdt\mathcal{E} = - \frac{N d\Phi B}{dt}E=−dtNdΦB​. For nonidentical linked fluxes, sum the flux linkages instead of assuming NΦN\PhiNΦ. The finite average magnitude is N∣ΔΦ∣Δt\frac{N \left| \Delta \Phi \right|}{\Delta t}ΔtN∣ΔΦ∣​; it equals the instantaneous value only for a constant rate during the interval.

E=−N(Acos⁡θdBdt+Bcos⁡θdAdt−BAsin⁡θdθdt).\mathcal E=-N\left(A\cos\theta\frac{dB}{dt}+B\cos\theta\frac{dA}{dt}-BA\sin\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right).E=−N(AcosθdtdB​+BcosθdtdA​−BAsinθdtdθ​).

This product-rule expression covers changing field strength, changing area, changing orientation, and simultaneous changes. Set only the quantities explicitly held constant to zero.

The source's 4.1 V4.1\,\mathrm{V}4.1V is rounded.

Lenz's law with four direction cases

Choose the external field direction, then determine whether its flux increases or decreases. The induced field OPPOSES THE CHANGE, not necessarily the external field. Use the right-hand grip rule to convert the required induced field into conventional current.

Motional emf from two derivations

Flux derivation. A rod of length ℓ slides distance dx in a perpendicular uniform B. The loop's area change is dA=ℓdxdA = \ell dxdA=ℓdx, so ∣E∣=Bℓ(dxdt)=Bℓv\left| \mathcal{E} \right| = B \ell \left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right) = B \ell v∣E∣=Bℓ(dtdx​)=Bℓv.

Charge-force derivation. Charges in an open moving rod redistribute until qE balances the magnetic qvB. Thus E=vBE = vBE=vB, and voltage magnitude Eℓ=BℓvE \ell = B \ell vEℓ=Bℓv. The general expression is ∫(v×B)⋅dl\int \left( v \times B \right) \cdot dl∫(v×B)⋅dl; the product Bℓv needs the stated perpendicular geometry.

For a sliding rod in a closed resistance R: I=BℓvRI = \frac{B \ell v}{R}I=RBℓv​. Magnetic drag magnitude is F=IℓB=B2ℓ2vRF = I \ell B = \frac{B^{2} \ell^{2} v}{R}F=IℓB=RB2ℓ2v​. Required mechanical power at constant speed is Fv=I2RFv = I^{2} RFv=I2R, which verifies energy conservation.

Worked example — primary p. 35. Speed 1000 kmh=277.778 ms\frac{1000\,\mathrm{km}}{h} = 277.778\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}h1000km​=277.778sm​. A 70 m70\,\mathrm{m}70m wingspan moving perpendicular to a nearly vertical 5.0×10−5 T5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}5.0×10−5T field develops about 0.9722 V0.9722\,\mathrm{V}0.9722V between tips. Which tip is positive depends on the velocity and field vector directions.

Generators, microphones, transformers, and eddy currents

For a rigid rotating N-turn coil, Φ=BAcos⁡(ωt+ϕ)\Phi = BA\cos \left( \omega t + \phi \right)Φ=BAcos(ωt+ϕ). Differentiate to derive E(t)=NBAωsin⁡(ωt+ϕ)\mathcal{E} \left( t \right) = NBA\omega \sin \left( \omega t + \phi \right)E(t)=NBAωsin(ωt+ϕ), with peak NBAωNBA\omegaNBAω. A GENERATOR converts mechanical input into electrical output. Primary p. 14 reverses that conversion in its wording; it describes motor action instead. A moving-coil microphone converts mechanical vibration into an electrical signal.

An ideal transformer links both windings to the same changing core flux. Dividing their Faraday equations gives VsVp=NsNp\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}Vp​Vs​​=Np​Ns​​. With ideal power conservation, VpIp=VsIsV_{p} I_{p} = V_{s} I_{s}Vp​Ip​=Vs​Is​ and IsIp=NpNs\frac{I_{s}}{I_{p}} = \frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}Ip​Is​​=Ns​Np​​. These are compatible AC magnitudes, usually rms values. A transformer does not directly convert AC into DC; a rectifier and other power-supply stages are required.

Worked example — primary p. 19. Ideal 120 V120\,\mathrm{V}120V to 9 V9\,\mathrm{V}9V AC, Ns=30N_{s} = 30Ns​=30, Is=0.400 AI_{s} = 0.400\,\mathrm{A}Is​=0.400A gives Np=400N_{p} = 400Np​=400 turns, output power: 3.6 W3.6\,\mathrm{W}3.6W, and input current: 0.030 A0.030\,\mathrm{A}0.030A. The slide's description of 9 V9\,\mathrm{V}9V DC includes an implicit rectifier; the transformer equations alone address the AC stage.

Eddy currents circulate in bulk conductors. Their opposing magnetic effects can slow moving metal. Energy becomes heat. A changing current in one coil can induce emf in a nearby coil even without a conducting connection between them.

Mutual/self-inductance and stored magnetic energy

Define mutual inductance through E2=−MdI1dt\mathcal{E}_{2} = - \frac{M dI_{1}}{dt}E2​=−dtMdI1​​. For a linear coil, flux linkage NΦ=LIN\Phi = LINΦ=LI, giving Eself=−LdIdt\mathcal{E} _{\mathrm{self}} = - \frac{L dI}{dt}Eself​=−dtLdI​. L and M have units henry: V⋅sA=Ω⋅s\frac{V \cdot s}{A} = \Omega \cdot sAV⋅s​=Ω⋅s. Constant permeability and fixed geometry are part of the simple constant-L model.

For an ideal long solenoid, B=μNIℓB = \frac{\mu NI}{\ell}B=ℓμNI​. Flux per turn is BA. Therefore L=NΦI=μN2AℓL = \frac{N\Phi}{I} = \frac{\mathrm{\mu N}^{2} A}{\ell}L=INΦ​=ℓμN2A​. Derive stored energy by P=LI(dIdt)P = LI \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)P=LI(dtdI​) and integrate: U=∫0ILidi=LI22U = \int_{0} ᴵ Li di = \frac{LI^{2}}{2}U=∫0I​Lidi=2LI2​. Inductors resist a CHANGE in current; they do not simply “oppose current” in every situation.

Substitute L=μN2AℓL = \frac{\mathrm{\mu N}^{2} A}{\ell}L=ℓμN2A​ into U=LI22U = \frac{LI^{2}}{2}U=2LI2​ and replace NIℓ\frac{NI}{\ell}ℓNI​ with Bμ\frac{B}{\mu}μB​. This gives U=B2Aℓ(2μ)U = \frac{B^{2} A \ell}{\left( 2 \mu \right)}U=(2μ)B2Aℓ​. Divide by the solenoid's internal field volume Aℓ to get magnetic energy density uB=B2(2μ)u_{B} = \frac{B^{2}}{\left( 2 \mu \right)}uB​=(2μ)B2​. Compare the electric result uE=εE22u_{E} = \frac{\varepsilon E^{2}}{2}uE​=2εE2​. Both formulas assume the specified linear material model.

RL growth, decay, and arbitrary initial current

KVL for an ideal L in series with total R gives E=L(dIdt)+RI\mathcal{E} = L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right) + RIE=L(dtdI​)+RI. Separate and integrate with I(0)=0I \left( 0 \right) = 0I(0)=0:

I(t)=ER(1−e−tR/L),τRL=L/R.I(t)=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}(1-e^{-tR/L}),\quad \tau_{RL}=L/R.I(t)=RE​(1−e−tR/L),τRL​=L/R.

After removing the source while retaining a closed R–L path, I=I0exp⁡(−tRL)I = I_{0} \exp \left( - \frac{t R}{L} \right)I=I0​exp(−LtR​). More generally I(t)=If+(I0−If)e−t/τI(t)=I_f+(I_0-I_f)e^{-t/\tau}I(t)=If​+(I0​−If​)e−t/τ. Inductor current is continuous in this ideal finite-voltage model. For fraction f of final growth, t=−(LR)ln⁡(1−f)t = - \left( \frac{L}{R} \right) \ln \left( 1 - f \right)t=−(RL​)ln(1−f). For remaining decay fraction f, t=−(LR)ln⁡ft = - \left( \frac{L}{R} \right) \ln ft=−(RL​)lnf. RC increases its time constant with R; RL decreases its time constant with R. Do not interchange them.

Switching check. A source-free decay needs a closed path. Opening the only path does not make a real inductor's current disappear without consequence. Its induced voltage can become large and cause a spark or flow through a protection component. The simple exponential requires a valid R–L discharge path.

Source problems · full working

Flux signs, partial overlap, and the induction experiment

Starting and stopping the primary-coil current — primary pp. 5–7. A steady primary current produces a steady field. A stationary secondary loop then has no transformer emf from that constant flux. Starting or stopping the primary current changes the shared flux and produces a secondary emf. The two coils need no conducting connection for this energy transfer.

Flux sign convention. Choose a surface normal first. A field component along that normal gives positive flux; the opposite component gives negative flux. Couple the positive loop direction to the normal by the right-hand grip rule. The Faraday minus sign then has a precise directional meaning.

  3. Reverse the surface normal to reverse the signed flux.

Check. BA1BA_{1}BA1​ would incorrectly assign a nonzero field to the whole loop interior. The relevant area is the area where field actually passes through the chosen surface.

Full Faraday and transformer solutions

Derivation∴

The AC generator waveform and rotation units

Source starting point: Primary p. 14. Let a rigid N-turn coil of area A rotate at constant angular speed ω\omegaω in a uniform field. Let θ\thetaθ be the angle between the area normal and B.

  1. Write θ(t)=ωt+ϕ\theta \left( t \right) = \omega t + \phiθ(t)=ωt+ϕ, with angles in radians.
  2. Write the flux per turn as Φ=BAcos⁡(ωt+ϕ)\Phi = BA\cos \left( \omega t + \phi \right)Φ=BAcos(ωt+ϕ).
  3. Differentiate the cosine: dΦdt=−BAωsin⁡(ωt+ϕ)\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = - BA\omega \sin \left( \omega t + \phi \right)dtdΦ​=−BAωsin(ωt+ϕ).
  4. Apply Faraday's minus sign and multiply by N.
E(t)=NBAωsin⁡(ωt+ϕ),Epeak=NBAω,ω=2πf.\mathcal E(t)=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi), \qquad \mathcal E_{peak}=NBA\omega, \qquad \omega=2\pi f.E(t)=NBAωsin(ωt+ϕ),Epeak​=NBAω,ω=2πf.

At maximum flux, the instantaneous flux slope and emf are zero. When the flux passes through zero during this rotation, the emf magnitude reaches its peak. Mechanical rotation supplies the electrical output energy. Do not substitute rotation frequency f in hertz directly for ω\omegaω in radians per second.

A step-up transformer increases voltage and decreases current for the same ideal transferred power. A step-down transformer does the reverse. Current does not travel across the insulation from one winding into the other. The changing magnetic field couples the circuits.

The missing distinction: induced electric fields are not electrostatic fields

Sources: Primary objectives on p. 23 and discussion on p. 34. A changing magnetic flux creates a circulating electric field. It can act on a charge initially at rest. A conducting wire is not required for the electric field to exist.

For electrostatics, a single-valued scalar potential gives E=−∇VE = - \nabla VE=−∇V and ∮E⋅dl=0\oint E \cdot dl = 0∮E⋅dl=0. In induction, the closed-loop integral can be nonzero:

∮E⋅dl=−dΦBdt.\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=-\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.∮E⋅dl=−dtdΦB​​.

The E=vBE = vBE=vB inside a moving open rod instead describes charge separation that balances qv×Bqv \times Bqv×B in that rod. It is not a universal formula for the circulating field around every changing magnetic field.

Derivation∴

Induced field inside and outside a circular changing-field region

This labeled extension develops the source objective. Let uniform B(t) point along +z inside radius a and be zero outside. Choose counterclockwise circulation as positive.

  1. By cylindrical symmetry, E is tangent to a centered circle and has constant magnitude along it.
  2. The circulation is Eϕ(2πr)E\phi \left( 2 \pi r \right)Eϕ(2πr).
  3. For r≤ar \le ar≤a, the enclosed magnetic flux is πr2B\pi r^{2} Bπr2B.
  4. For r≥ar \ge ar≥a, the enclosed magnetic flux is πa2B\pi a^{2} Bπa2B.
  5. Apply Faraday's law and solve each region separately.
Eϕ(r)={−r2dBdt,r≤a,−a22rdBdt,r≥a.E_\phi(r)=\begin{cases} -\dfrac r2\dfrac{dB}{dt},&r\le a,\\[6pt] -\dfrac{a^2}{2r}\dfrac{dB}{dt},&r\ge a. \end{cases}Eϕ​(r)=⎩⎨⎧​−2r​dtdB​,−2ra2​dtdB​,​r≤a,r≥a.​

Checks. Both expressions agree at r=ar = ar=a. E tends to zero at the center. Outside, E can remain nonzero even where the local magnetic field is zero, because the loop encloses changing flux. For increasing +z flux, EϕE\phiEϕ is negative, so the circulation is clockwise.

Mutual inductance, self-inductance, and complete RL decay

Derivation∴

Derive self-inductance from flux linkage

Sources: Primary pp. 37–41. For a linear coil, the total linkage is Λ=NΦ=LI\Lambda = N\Phi = LIΛ=NΦ=LI. If L is constant, differentiation gives dΛdt=L(dIdt)\frac{d \Lambda}{dt} = L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)dtdΛ​=L(dtdI​). Faraday's law therefore gives Eself=−L(dIdt)\mathcal{E} _{\mathrm{self}} = - L \left( \frac{dI}{dt} \right)Eself​=−L(dtdI​).

For a long solenoid, substitute B=μNIℓB = \frac{\mu NI}{\ell}B=ℓμNI​ into Φ=BA\Phi = BAΦ=BA:

L=NΦI=N(μNI/ℓ)AI=μN2Aℓ.L=\frac{N\Phi}{I} =\frac{N(\mu NI/\ell)A}{I} =\frac{\mu N^2A}{\ell}.L=INΦ​=IN(μNI/ℓ)A​=ℓμN2A​.

For mutual inductance, use Λ2=N2Φ21=MI1\Lambda_{2} = N_{2} \Phi_{21} = MI_{1}Λ2​=N2​Φ21​=MI1​, so E2=−M(dI1dt)\mathcal{E}_{2} = - M \left( \frac{dI_{1}}{dt} \right)E2​=−M(dtdI1​​) for constant geometry and a linear material. A steady current gives no induced emf from these constant-linkage terms.

Module 10 / Physics 2

Light and optics: measure angles from the normal

Light, photons, reflection, Snell law, critical angles, and fibers.

Topics in this module
Wave quantities and wavelength conversionPhoton energy and a necessary source correctionReflection and surfacesSnell's law: derive it from phase matchingSeveral interfaces and the water–glass–air answerCritical angle and total internal reflectionExam-scope noteWavelengths, refractive index, and the source's physical modelsPhotoelectric equations with the unit conversions shownReflection and refraction: complete the source angle calculationsTotal internal reflection, optical fibers, and useful inverse forms

Electromagnetic waves in vacuum satisfy c=fλc = f\lambdac=fλ, with c=299,792,458 msc = 299{,}792{,}458\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=299,792,458sm​ exactly. Use 3.00×108 ms3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}3.00×108sm​ when the problem's precision supports that rounding. In a medium, v=cnv = \frac{c}{n}v=nc​ and v=fλmediumv = f\lambda _{\mathrm{medium}}v=fλmedium​. The frequency stays the same across a stationary interface; speed and wavelength can change.

Wave quantities and wavelength conversion

λ0=c/f,f=c/λ0,n=c/v,λmedium=λ0/n.\lambda_0=c/f,\quad f=c/\lambda_0,\quad n=c/v,\quad \lambda_{medium}=\lambda_0/n.λ0​=c/f,f=c/λ0​,n=c/v,λmedium​=λ0​/n.

Worked example — primary p. 8. With c=3.00×108 msc = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=3.00×108sm​, 4.0×1014 Hz4.0 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}4.0×1014Hz corresponds to 750 nm750\,\mathrm{nm}750nm. A frequency of 7.9×1014 Hz7.9 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}7.9×1014Hz corresponds to about 380 nm380\,\mathrm{nm}380nm. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength in the same medium. Convert 1 nm=10−9 m1\,\mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}1nm=10−9m before calculating energy or speed.

The source introduces Newton's particle account, Huygens' wave account, and Young's interference evidence. Modern light has wave and particle behavior; neither everyday particles nor classical waves alone explain all observations. Ray optics approximates propagation by rays when wavelength is small compared with the relevant geometry.

Photon energy and a necessary source correction

Eγ=hf=hc/λ0,Kmax=hf−ϕ,f0=ϕ/h,eVstop=Kmax.E_\gamma=hf=hc/\lambda_0,\quad K_{max}=hf-\phi,\quad f_0=\phi/h,\quad eV_{stop}=K_{max}.Eγ​=hf=hc/λ0​,Kmax​=hf−ϕ,f0​=ϕ/h,eVstop​=Kmax​.

The source introduces E=hfE = hfE=hf. The photoelectric relations above extend that idea to explain its experiment correctly. Photon energy must first supply work function ϕ\phiϕ; excess energy becomes maximum electron kinetic energy. If hf<ϕhf < \phihf<ϕ, the model predicts no single-photon photoemission regardless of ordinary intensity increases.

Primary p. 10 incorrectly says electron kinetic energy is independent of frequency. Maximum kinetic energy INCREASES with frequency above threshold. At fixed frequency, higher intensity increases available photon rate, not each photon's energy. See the supplementary photoelectric reference in the source notes.

Worked extension. At λ=500 nm\lambda = 500\,\mathrm{nm}λ=500nm, Eγ=(6.626×10−34)(3.00×108)(500×10−9)=3.976×10−19 J≈2.482 eV\begin{aligned}E_{\gamma} &= \frac{\left( 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \right) \left( 3.00 \times 10^{8} \right)}{\left( 500 \times 10^{-9} \right)} \\&= 3.976 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J} \approx 2.482\,\mathrm{eV}\end{aligned}Eγ​​=(500×10−9)(6.626×10−34)(3.00×108)​=3.976×10−19J≈2.482eV​ For ϕ=2.00 eV\phi = 2.00\,\mathrm{eV}ϕ=2.00eV, Kmax≈0.482 eVK_{\mathrm{max}} \approx 0.482\,\mathrm{eV}Kmax​≈0.482eV and stopping-potential magnitude ≈ 0.482 V0.482\,\mathrm{V}0.482V. The boundary wavelength hcϕ\frac{hc}{\phi}ϕhc​ is about 620 nm620\,\mathrm{nm}620nm. A longer wavelength cannot supply the required photon energy in this model.

Reflection and surfaces

The law of reflection is θr=θiθ_{r} = θ_{i}θr​=θi​, with both angles measured from the surface NORMAL. A 30° angle to the surface is a 60° incidence angle. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in one plane. A smooth surface gives specular reflection; a rough surface gives diffuse reflection through differing local normals. Diffuse reflection does not mean each microscopic reflection violates the law.

Derivation extension — stationary travel time. For a reflection point sliding along a flat mirror in one uniform medium, total travel time is proportional to the sum of incoming and outgoing path lengths. Differentiate that sum with respect to the reflection point. Setting its derivative to zero gives equal sine ratios and hence θi=θrθ_{i} = θ_{r}θi​=θr​ in the ordinary reflection range.

Let the endpoints have horizontal separation d and heights h1h_{1}h1​,h2h_{2}h2​ above the mirror. Put the reflection point at horizontal coordinate x. The path length is (x2+h12)+((d−x)2+h22)\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)} + \sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}(x2+h12​)​+((d−x)2+h22​)​. Its derivative vanishes when x(x2+h12)=(d−x)((d−x)2+h22)\frac{x}{\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)}} = \frac{\left( d - x \right)}{\sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}}(x2+h12​)​x​=((d−x)2+h22​)​(d−x)​. These ratios are sin⁡θi\sin θ_{i}sinθi​ and sin⁡θr\sin θ_{r}sinθr​, measured from the vertical normal. Their equality gives the reflection law.

Snell's law: derive it from phase matching

At a stationary planar boundary, the wave phase must agree along the interface. Tangential wavevector components match: k1sin⁡θ1=k2sin⁡θ2k_{1} \sin \theta_{1} = k_{2} \sin \theta_{2}k1​sinθ1​=k2​sinθ2​. Since k=2πnλ0k = \frac{2 \pi n}{\lambda_{0}}k=λ0​2πn​ at a common frequency:

n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2,θ2=sin⁡−1(n1n2sin⁡θ1).n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2,\quad \theta_2=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n_1}{n_2}\sin\theta_1\right).n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​,θ2​=sin−1(n2​n1​​sinθ1​).

Rearrange to n2=n1sin⁡θ1sin⁡θ2n_{2} = \frac{n_{1} \sin \theta_{1}}{\sin \theta_{2}}n2​=sinθ2​n1​sinθ1​​ or θ1=sin⁡−1(n2sin⁡θ2n1)\theta_{1} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{n_{2} \sin \theta_{2}}{n_{1}} \right)θ1​=sin−1(n1​n2​sinθ2​​) when the physical domain permits. The sine argument must lie between −1 and +1. In the ordinary incidence range, n2>n1n_{2} > n_{1}n2​>n1​ bends toward the normal; n2<n1n_{2} < n_{1}n2​<n1​ bends away. At normal incidence, direction stays normal although speed and wavelength can change.

Independent derivation extension — stationary time. With one endpoint above and the other below the interface, travel time is t(x)=(n1c)(x2+h12)+(n2c)((d−x)2+h22)t \left( x \right) = \left( \frac{n_{1}}{c} \right) \sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)} + \left( \frac{n_{2}}{c} \right) \sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}t(x)=(cn1​​)(x2+h12​)​+(cn2​​)((d−x)2+h22​)​. Differentiate with respect to x. Setting dtdx=0\frac{dt}{dx} = 0dxdt​=0 gives n1sin⁡θ1−n2sin⁡θ2=0n_{1} \sin \theta_{1} - n_{2} \sin \theta_{2} = 0n1​sinθ1​−n2​sinθ2​=0. This reproduces Snell's law without assuming equal speeds in the two media. It applies to the stated uniform, stationary media and planar boundary.

Worked example — primary p. 25. Air n1=1.00n_{1} = 1.00n1​=1.00 to water n2=1.33n_{2} = 1.33n2​=1.33, θ1=45∘\theta_{1} = 45^{\circ}θ1​=45∘. θ2=sin⁡−1(sin⁡45∘1.33)≈32.12∘\theta_{2} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{1.33} \right) \approx 32.12^{\circ}θ2​=sin−1(1.33sin45∘​)≈32.12∘. A value measured from the surface would be its complement.

Several interfaces and the water–glass–air answer

For parallel boundaries, the refracted angle inside the middle layer equals its incidence angle at the next boundary. Applying Snell twice gives n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2=n3sin⁡θ3n_{1} \sin \theta_{1} = n_{2} \sin \theta_{2} = n_{3} \sin \theta_{3}n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​=n3​sinθ3​. The middle index cancels from the final angle relation, but not from the internal angle or lateral displacement.

Worked correction — primary pp. 26–27. Water n=1.3n = 1.3n=1.3, glass n=1.5n = 1.5n=1.5, air n=1.0n = 1.0n=1.0; start at 20° from the normal in water. Reflection in water gives θA=20∘\theta_{A} = 20^{\circ}θA​=20∘. Glass refraction gives θB=sin⁡−1[(1.31.5)sin⁡20∘]≈17.24∘\theta_{B} = \sin^{-1} \left[ \left( \frac{1.3}{1.5} \right) \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 17.24^{\circ}θB​=sin−1[(1.51.3​)sin20∘]≈17.24∘. For parallel faces θC=17.24∘\theta_{C} = 17.24^{\circ}θC​=17.24∘. Exit into air gives θD=sin⁡−1[1.3sin⁡20∘]≈26.40∘\theta_{D} = \sin^{-1} \left[ 1.3 \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 26.40^{\circ}θD​=sin−1[1.3sin20∘]≈26.40∘, not the printed 20°. Returning to the original angle would require equal first and final indices, which this drawing does not have.

Parallel-slab extension. For slab thickness t, internal angle r, and external incidence i, perpendicular lateral displacement is s=tsin⁡(i−r)cos⁡rs = \frac{t \sin \left( i - r \right)}{\cos} rs=costsin(i−r)​r. Derive it by drawing the internal path of length tcos⁡r\frac{t}{\cos} rcost​r and projecting its deviation from the original ray. This formula assumes parallel faces and an exit into the original medium without total internal reflection.

Critical angle and total internal reflection

Set the transmitted angle to 90° in Snell's law:

sin⁡θc=n2/n1,θc=sin⁡−1(n2/n1),n1>n2.\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1,\quad \theta_c=\sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1),\quad n_1>n_2.sinθc​=n2​/n1​,θc​=sin−1(n2​/n1​),n1​>n2​.

Total internal reflection requires travel from larger n to smaller n AND θi>θcθ_{i} > θ_{c}θi​>θc​. At θi=θcθ_{i} = θ_{c}θi​=θc​, the ideal refracted ray grazes the boundary; it is the threshold, not a greater-angle case. If n1≤n2n_{1} \le n_{2}n1​≤n2​, there is no real critical angle for this direction of travel.

Worked example. Glass n=1.50n = 1.50n=1.50 to air n=1.00n = 1.00n=1.00 gives θc≈41.81∘θ_{c} \approx 41.81^{\circ}θc​≈41.81∘. At 30°, refraction remains possible. At 50°, Snell's proposed transmitted sine exceeds one, so no propagating refracted ray exists in the elementary model. Use reflection rather than reporting a complex physical ray angle.

An optical fiber uses a higher-index core and lower-index cladding. Suitable core rays meet the boundary above its critical angle. The ideal ray picture guides them by total internal reflection. Real fibers still have attenuation, absorption, scattering, and bend losses; primary p. 31's “no absorption” wording is an idealization.

Fiber acceptance extension. In the meridional-ray model, let n0n_{0}n0​ be the entrance-medium index, ncore the core index, and nclad the cladding index. For a ray inside the core at angle θ\thetaθ to its axis, wall incidence is 90∘−θ90^{\circ} - \theta90∘−θ. At the limiting ray, cos⁡θ=ncladncore\cos \theta = \frac{n_{\mathrm{clad}}}{n_{\mathrm{core}}}cosθ=ncore​nclad​​. Use sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^{2} \theta + \cos^{2} \theta = 1sin2θ+cos2θ=1, then apply Snell at the flat entrance:

n0sin⁡θaccept=ncore2−nclad2=NA.n_0\sin\theta_{accept}=\sqrt{n_{core}^2-n_{clad}^2}=NA.n0​sinθaccept​=ncore2​−nclad2​​=NA.

For a core index 1.48 and cladding index 1.46, NA≈0.24249NA \approx 0.24249NA≈0.24249. From air, the limiting entrance half-angle is about 14.03°. This is an angle to the fiber AXIS at the entrance, not the wall incidence angle. This ideal extension does not describe every skew ray, bend, or waveguide mode.

Exam-scope note

The supplied Module 10 ends with reflection, refraction, and total internal reflection. It does not supply a complete thin-lens/mirror, diffraction, or polarization course. Extensions above are labeled. No finite set contains every possible derivation; these notes cover the supplied laws, standard inversions, limiting cases, and explicitly stated extensions. Always check the problem's geometry, physical assumptions, and available data before selecting an equation.

Source problems · full working

Wavelengths, refractive index, and the source's physical models

Source context — primary pp. 4–11. All electromagnetic frequencies travel at c in vacuum. Visible light forms only a small part of the spectrum. Newton's historical particle description and Huygens' wave description precede modern wave–particle behavior. Young's interference experiment supports wave behavior. Einstein's photoelectric explanation connects photon energy to frequency.

Ray approximation. Rays describe propagation directions in geometric optics. In a uniform medium they travel along straight lines. In a medium with a varying refractive index, they can curve. The approximation works when the wavelength is small relative to the relevant geometric features. A ray is not a literal thin material strand.

Worked solution↳

Visible-light frequency range to wavelength range

Source: Primary p. 8. Given: f ranges from 4.0×10144.0 \times 10^{14}4.0×1014 to 7.9×1014 Hz7.9 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}7.9×1014Hz. Use c=3.00×108 msc = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=3.00×108sm​.

  1. Start with c=fλc = f\lambdac=fλ and isolate λ=cf\lambda = \frac{c}{f}λ=fc​.
  2. Use the lowest frequency for the longest wavelength: λmax=3.00×108(4.0×1014)=7.50×10−7 m\begin{aligned}\lambda _{\mathrm{max}} &= \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{\left( 4.0 \times 10^{14} \right)} \\&= 7.50 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}\end{aligned}λmax​​=(4.0×1014)3.00×108​=7.50×10−7m​
  3. Convert meters to nanometers: 7.50×10−7×109=750 nm7.50 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{9} = 750\,\mathrm{nm}7.50×10−7×109=750nm.
  4. Use the highest frequency for the shortest wavelength: λmin=3.00×108(7.9×1014)≈3.79747×10−7 m=379.747 nm\begin{aligned}\lambda _{\mathrm{min}} &= \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{\left( 7.9 \times 10^{14} \right)} \approx 3.79747 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m} \\&= 379.747\,\mathrm{nm}\end{aligned}λmin​​=(7.9×1014)3.00×108​≈3.79747×10−7m=379.747nm​
  5. Report about 380–750 nm750\,\mathrm{nm}750nm in increasing wavelength order.

Check. Increasing frequency decreases wavelength. Reversing the endpoint order without stating the inverse relation makes the interval misleading.

The table gives air 1.0003, ice 1.31, water 1.33, alcohol 1.36, fused quartz 1.46, crown glass 1.52, and diamond 2.42. Refractive index depends on material conditions and wavelength. The later water–glass–air exercise explicitly uses 1.3, 1.5, and 1.0 instead. Use those stated exercise values.

Derivation∴

Frequency stays fixed while speed and wavelength change

At a stationary interface, the oscillation rate must match on both sides. Otherwise, the boundary phase cannot remain matched over time. Thus f1=f2f_{1} = f_{2}f1​=f2​. Use v=fλv = f\lambdav=fλ and n=cvn = \frac{c}{v}n=vc​:

λ2λ1=v2v1=n1n2,λmedium=λ0n.\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}=\frac{v_2}{v_1}=\frac{n_1}{n_2}, \qquad \lambda_{medium}=\frac{\lambda_0}{n}.λ1​λ2​​=v1​v2​​=n2​n1​​,λmedium​=nλ0​​.

For a labeled example, 600 nm600\,\mathrm{nm}600nm vacuum light entering n=1.50n = 1.50n=1.50 glass has v=2.00×108 msv = 2.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}v=2.00×108sm​ and λglass=400 nm\lambda _{\mathrm{glass}} = 400\,\mathrm{nm}λglass​=400nm. Its frequency remains 5.00×1014 Hz5.00 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}5.00×1014Hz. The shorter in-glass wavelength does not mean the photon acquires a higher frequency at this stationary boundary.

Photoelectric equations with the unit conversions shown

Worked solution↳

Photon energy, kinetic energy, and stopping voltage

Source starting point: Primary p. 10 introduces Eγ=hfE_{\gamma} = hfEγ​=hf. The work-function and stopping-voltage calculations are labeled extensions.

Given: λ0=500 nm\lambda_{0} = 500\,\mathrm{nm}λ0​=500nm, ϕ=2.00 eV\phi = 2.00\,\mathrm{eV}ϕ=2.00eV, h=6.626×10−34 J⋅sh = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J} \cdot sh=6.626×10−34J⋅s, c=3.00×108 msc = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}c=3.00×108sm​, and 1 eV=1.602×10−19 J1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}1eV=1.602×10−19J.

  1. Convert λ0=500×10−9 m\lambda_{0} = 500 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}λ0​=500×10−9m.
  2. Calculate Eγ=hcλ0=3.9756×10−19 JE_{\gamma} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{0}} = 3.9756 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}Eγ​=λ0​hc​=3.9756×10−19J.
  3. Convert to electronvolts: Eγ=3.97561.602=2.48165 eVE_{\gamma} = \frac{3.9756}{1.602} = 2.48165\,\mathrm{eV}Eγ​=1.6023.9756​=2.48165eV.
  4. Subtract the work function in the same unit: Kmax=2.48165−2.00=0.481648 eVK_{\mathrm{max}} = 2.48165 - 2.00 = 0.481648\,\mathrm{eV}Kmax​=2.48165−2.00=0.481648eV.
  5. Divide Kmax in joules by e to obtain a stopping-potential magnitude of 0.481648 V0.481648\,\mathrm{V}0.481648V.
  6. Use λthreshold=hcϕ≈620.4 nm\lambda thresh_{\mathrm{old}} = \frac{hc}{\phi} \approx 620.4\,\mathrm{nm}λthreshold​=ϕhc​≈620.4nm with these rounded constants.

Check. An energy of one electronvolt equals e times a potential difference of one volt. It is an energy unit, not a voltage unit. Here λ0\lambda_{0}λ0​ is shorter than the threshold wavelength, so single-photon emission is energetically possible.

Derivation∴

Threshold and stopping-potential rearrangements

Use conservation of energy for one emitted electron: hf=ϕ+Kmaxhf = \phi + K_{\mathrm{max}}hf=ϕ+Kmax​. At threshold, Kmax=0K_{\mathrm{max}} = 0Kmax​=0, so f0=ϕhf_{0} = \frac{\phi}{h}f0​=hϕ​. With vacuum wavelength λ0=cf\lambda_{0} = \frac{c}{f}λ0​=fc​, the longest threshold wavelength is λthreshold=hcϕ\lambda thresh_{\mathrm{old}} = \frac{hc}{\phi}λthreshold​=ϕhc​.

For the stopping-potential magnitude, eVstop=KmaxeV_{\mathrm{stop}} = K_{\mathrm{max}}eVstop​=Kmax​. Therefore:

Vstop=hef−ϕe,ϕ=hf−eVstop.V_{stop}=\frac he f-\frac\phi e, \qquad \phi=hf-eV_{stop}.Vstop​=eh​f−eϕ​,ϕ=hf−eVstop​.

A Vstop-versus-frequency graph has slope he\frac{h}{e}eh​ and a zero-voltage intercept at f0f_{0}f0​. At fixed frequency above threshold, ordinary intensity changes affect photon arrival rate rather than each photon's energy. Primary p. 10's frequency-independent kinetic-energy statement is incorrect.

Reflection and refraction: complete the source angle calculations

Reflection geometry. Measure the incident and reflected angles from the same surface normal. If the incident ray is 30° above a flat surface, its incidence angle is 60°. Its reflected ray is also 60° from the normal, or 30° from the surface. Diffuse reflection comes from different microscopic normal directions on a rough surface; it does not replace the local reflection law.

Derivation∴

Reflection from a stationary-path calculation

Let the endpoints lie at heights h1h_{1}h1​ and h2h_{2}h2​ above a horizontal mirror, separated horizontally by d. Let the reflection point have horizontal coordinate x. In the same uniform medium, minimizing travel time also makes the optical path stationary.

L(x)=x2+h12+(d−x)2+h22.L(x)=\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2}+\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}.L(x)=x2+h12​​+(d−x)2+h22​​.
  1. Differentiate: dLdx=x(x2+h12)−(d−x)((d−x)2+h22)\frac{dL}{dx} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\left( x^{2} + h_{1}^{2} \right)}} - \frac{\left( d - x \right)}{\sqrt{\left( \left( d - x \right)^{2} + h_{2}^{2} \right)}}dxdL​=(x2+h12​)​x​−((d−x)2+h22​)​(d−x)​.
  2. Set dLdx=0\frac{dL}{dx} = 0dxdL​=0.
  3. Recognize the two ratios as sin⁡θi\sin θ_{i}sinθi​ and sin⁡θr\sin θ_{r}sinθr​, with angles from the normal.
  4. Obtain sin⁡θi=sin⁡θr\sin θ_{i} = \sin θ_{r}sinθi​=sinθr​. For ordinary reflection angles between 0° and 90°, θi=θrθ_{i} = θ_{r}θi​=θr​.

This is a labeled derivation of the source's reflection law, not a new mirror-image equation.

Derivation∴

Snell's law from stationary travel time

For endpoints in two uniform media separated by a flat interface, write:

t(x)=n1cx2+h12+n2c(d−x)2+h22.t(x)=\frac{n_1}{c}\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2} +\frac{n_2}{c}\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}.t(x)=cn1​​x2+h12​​+cn2​​(d−x)2+h22​​.
  1. Differentiate with respect to the crossing position x.
  2. Set dtdx=0\frac{dt}{dx} = 0dxdt​=0 and multiply by c.
  3. Replace the geometric ratios by the sines of the normal-based angles.
n1xx2+h12−n2d−x(d−x)2+h22=0⇒n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2.n_1\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+h_1^2}} -n_2\frac{d-x}{\sqrt{(d-x)^2+h_2^2}}=0 \Rightarrow n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2.n1​x2+h12​​x​−n2​(d−x)2+h22​​d−x​=0⇒n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​.

The same law follows from matching tangential wavevector components. Both derivations assume stationary media and a stationary planar interface. Different speeds require the n-weighted travel time; minimizing the unweighted geometric length would give the wrong refraction law.

Worked solution↳

Air into water at 45°

Source: Primary p. 25. Use n1=1.00n_{1} = 1.00n1​=1.00 for air and n2=1.33n_{2} = 1.33n2​=1.33 for water.

  1. Write 1.00sin⁡45∘=1.33sin⁡θ21.00 \sin 45^{\circ} = 1.33 \sin \theta_{2}1.00sin45∘=1.33sinθ2​.
  2. Divide by 1.33: sin⁡θ2=0.531659\sin \theta_{2} = 0.531659sinθ2​=0.531659.
  3. Use inverse sine in degree mode: θ2≈32.1176∘\theta_{2} \approx 32.1176^{\circ}θ2​≈32.1176∘.
  4. Report about 32.1° from the normal.

Check. The ray enters the higher-index medium and bends toward the normal, so its normal-based angle decreases. Do not multiply the angle 45° directly by an index ratio.

Worked solution↳

Water, glass, and air: calculate all four requested angles

Sources: Primary pp. 26–27. Given: Water n=1.3n = 1.3n=1.3, glass n=1.5n = 1.5n=1.5, air n=1.0n = 1.0n=1.0, and initial incidence 20° from the normal.

  1. Reflection in water gives θA=20∘\theta_{A} = 20^{\circ}θA​=20∘.
  2. Apply Snell at the first boundary: 1.3sin⁡20∘=1.5sin⁡θB1.3 \sin 20^{\circ} = 1.5 \sin \theta_{B}1.3sin20∘=1.5sinθB​.
  3. Calculate θB=sin⁡−1[(1.31.5)sin⁡20∘]≈17.2426∘\theta_{B} = \sin^{-1} \left[ \left( \frac{1.3}{1.5} \right) \sin 20^{\circ} \right] \approx 17.2426^{\circ}θB​=sin−1[(1.51.3​)sin20∘]≈17.2426∘.
  4. Use the parallel glass faces: θC=θB≈17.2426∘\theta_{C} = \theta_{B} \approx 17.2426^{\circ}θC​=θB​≈17.2426∘.
  5. Apply Snell at the second boundary: 1.5sin⁡θC=1.0sin⁡θD1.5 \sin \theta_{C} = 1.0 \sin \theta_{D}1.5sinθC​=1.0sinθD​.
  6. Substitute the first-boundary relation to avoid early rounding: sin⁡θD=1.3sin⁡20∘\sin \theta_{D} = 1.3 \sin 20^{\circ}sinθD​=1.3sin20∘.
  7. Calculate θD≈26.3994∘\theta_{D} \approx 26.3994^{\circ}θD​≈26.3994∘.

Source correction. The printed exit angle 20° is incorrect for the stated first and final indices. Parallel faces restore the original angle only when the first and final media have the same refractive index. Check each interface for total internal reflection before applying a transmitted-ray formula.

Total internal reflection, optical fibers, and useful inverse forms

Derivation∴

Critical angle and the domain test

Sources: Primary pp. 22 and 28–31. At the threshold, the refracted angle is 90°. Insert it into Snell's law:

n1sin⁡θc=n2sin⁡90∘=n2⇒θc=sin⁡−1(n2n1).n_1\sin\theta_c=n_2\sin90^\circ=n_2 \Rightarrow\theta_c=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right).n1​sinθc​=n2​sin90∘=n2​⇒θc​=sin−1(n1​n2​​).
  1. Check n1>n2n_{1} > n_{2}n1​>n2​. Without a higher-to-lower index transition, there is no ordinary critical angle.
  2. Calculate θcθ_{c}θc​ from the normal.
  3. Compare the actual incidence angle with θcθ_{c}θc​.
  4. Use refraction for θi<θcθ_{i} < θ_{c}θi​<θc​, a grazing transmitted ray at θi=θcθ_{i} = θ_{c}θi​=θc​, and total internal reflection for θi>θcθ_{i} > θ_{c}θi​>θc​.

If sin⁡θ2=(n1n2)sin⁡θ1\sin \theta_{2} = \left( \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} \right) \sin \theta_{1}sinθ2​=(n2​n1​​)sinθ1​ exceeds one, no real propagating refracted ray satisfies this elementary model. Do not force the calculator to return a transmitted angle.

Worked solution↳

Glass–air and water–air thresholds

Labeled numerical extensions of the source law.

  1. For n1=1.50n_{1} = 1.50n1​=1.50 glass and n2=1.00n_{2} = 1.00n2​=1.00 air, θc=sin⁡−1(11.50)=41.8103∘θ_{c} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1.50} \right) = 41.8103^{\circ}θc​=sin−1(1.501​)=41.8103∘.
  2. At θi=30∘θ_{i} = 30^{\circ}θi​=30∘, sin⁡θ2=1.50sin⁡30∘=0.75\sin \theta_{2} = 1.50 \sin 30^{\circ} = 0.75sinθ2​=1.50sin30∘=0.75, so θ2≈48.5904∘\theta_{2} \approx 48.5904^{\circ}θ2​≈48.5904∘.
  3. At θi=50∘θ_{i} = 50^{\circ}θi​=50∘, the proposed transmitted sine is 1.14907>11.14907 > 11.14907>1. Total internal reflection occurs.
  4. For water n=1.33n = 1.33n=1.33 to air, θc=sin⁡−1(11.33)≈48.7535∘θ_{c} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{1.33} \right) \approx 48.7535^{\circ}θc​=sin−1(1.331​)≈48.7535∘.

Check. Reversing the direction to air → glass removes the total-internal-reflection condition. An “optically denser” medium means a larger refractive index here, not necessarily a larger mass density.

Fiber applications — primary pp. 30–31. A higher-index core and lower-index cladding support total internal reflection for suitable rays. Fiber links carry information encoded in light. The source lists telephone and internet links, cable systems, medical imaging, and engineering inspection. Real fibers have losses from absorption, scattering, and bending. The cladding's role is optical confinement; it does not make every fiber perfectly lossless.

Derivation∴

Apparent depth at a flat surface: a labeled small-angle extension

Let an object lie a true depth h inside index n1n_{1}n1​. An observer in index n2n_{2}n2​ extends a refracted ray backward and sees apparent depth happ.

  1. Draw a ray reaching the interface at horizontal offset x. Then tan⁡θ1=xh\tan \theta_{1} = \frac{x}{h}tanθ1​=hx​ and tan⁡θ2=x\tan \theta_{2} = xtanθ2​=x/happ.
  2. For small normal-based angles, use sin⁡θ≈tan⁡θ≈θ\sin \theta \approx \tan \theta \approx \thetasinθ≈tanθ≈θ in radians.
  3. Insert the geometric ratios into Snell's law: n1xh≈n2x\frac{n_{1} x}{h} \approx n_{2} xhn1​x​≈n2​x/happ.
  4. Cancel x and solve happ ≈ h(n2n1)h \left( \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} \right)h(n1​n2​​).

For a 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m deep object in water n1=1.33n_{1} = 1.33n1​=1.33 viewed from air n2=1.00n_{2} = 1.00n2​=1.00, happ ≈ 0.752 m0.752\,\mathrm{m}0.752m. The small-angle restriction matters. This extension does not replace exact ray tracing at a large viewing angle.
